## 47. Principles of growth

*Agreed on 17 October. Extends entries 40 and 45 and document 18.*

**Before.** The rules mixed constants and formulas without saying which values must change as the network grows. Nothing kept a rule
from making the work of every super-node grow with the size of the whole network, overload was counted by deals alone (entry 40), and
nothing said what happens when the network reaches a limit that no rule can move.

**Now.** Five principles. Every later rule is checked against them.
- **A formula, not a number, for whatever depends on size.** A value that depends on the size of the network is a formula of what the
  contracts see — receipts, redeemed search and delivery vouchers, the registry of super-nodes. Bitcoin works this way: every 2016 blocks
  it recomputes its difficulty so that a block still comes about every ten minutes, whatever the computing power of the network.
  Ethereum moves its base fee every block towards a target (EIP-1559). The values that express the mission — the fee ceiling, the price
  of a search, the price of a delivered message — stay constants.
- **The work of one super-node stays bounded.** No rule may make each super-node do work in proportion to the number of all agents or
  all super-nodes. Work that grows with the network is divided into parts that anyone can compute from the registry, and the network
  meets growth by adding super-nodes. What one super-node must carry may still rise (entry 45), but not in proportion to the whole
  network.
- **Overload counts all the work the contracts see.** New places open under overload (entry 40) when deals, redeemed searches or
  delivered messages per super-node exceed their constants, not deals alone.
- **Few transactions per deal.** Whatever can be settled in a batch is settled in a batch, as search vouchers already are: the
  throughput of the blockchain is a limit that no formula in a contract can move.
- **A limit no formula moves is passed by a new version.** When the network reaches such a limit — the throughput of one blockchain
  network above all — it grows through a new version of the contracts, possibly on several networks, which participants adopt of their
  own will (document 18, section 18.3). Reputation stays bound to the element.

**Why.** The network is meant to serve billions of agents years from now, on hardware nobody can measure today. A model of that load
built on today's machines would prove nothing. What can be checked today is the shape of the rules: whether the work of each super-node
stays bounded as the network grows. An unchanging rule can serve a network many orders of magnitude larger than at its start when it
adapts by formula, as Bitcoin's difficulty shows. Modelling therefore checks every rule as the load on one super-node as a function of
the size of the network, not as the capacity of a given year.

**Documents:** 05, 18; README; README of `lagrix-supernode`.

## 48. Announcements reach the super-nodes that hold them; a new super-node catches up

*Agreed on 17 October. Extends entries 30, 32 and 40; applies entry 47.*

**Before.** Announcements travelled over Nostr. Every super-node ran its own relay or subscribed to relays, gathered announcements into
its own index and declared which relays it read (entry 32, documents 17 and 18). Nothing said where a node should publish so that the
super-nodes see its agents, how a super-node learns the relays of the others, how a new super-node fills its empty index, or whether
the completeness of an index is checked. A super-node that was missing an agent could always say it had never received the
announcement, and section 17.3, which forbids dropping one agent inside a declared kind, had nothing to compare against.

**Now.**
- **Every super-node runs a relay, recorded with its place.** When a super-node registers its place in SuperNodeRegistry, it records the
  address of its Nostr relay; only the wallet that holds the place can change it. The relay's information document (NIP-11) carries the
  super-node's declaration (document 18, section 18.4). The list of super-nodes and their relays is read from the contract; nobody keeps
  a list of their own.
- **Each kind of service has holders that anyone can compute.** A kind of service — the capability (tag `c`) a customer searches
  for — is held by the k super-nodes whose keys are closest to the key of that kind of service, counting only super-nodes whose declared
  restrictions do not exclude it
  (section 17.9); k is a constant. Anyone computes the holders from the registry and the declarations; nobody assigns them. While no more
  than k super-nodes cover a kind, all of them hold it. As super-nodes join, each holds a smaller share of all kinds, and no rule has to
  change.
- **Any super-node may hold more.** Beyond its duty, a super-node may add any kind to its coverage. The search fee goes to the super-node
  that built the result list (section 17.8), so the kinds people search for most draw more holders by themselves.
- **A node publishes to the holders of its kinds.** A node publishes each announcement and each update to the relays of the holders of
  its kinds, and may add any other relay. Publishing costs nothing: a super-node's relay takes announcements free of charge.
- **Holders copy from each other.** Every holder keeps a subscription (NIP-01) to the relays of the other holders of the same kind,
  checks the author's signature on each announcement and keeps it on its own relay. An announcement that reached one holder reaches the
  others, even if its node has gone offline since. A super-node never copies from all super-nodes, only from the holders of its kinds.
- **A new super-node catches up before its check.** Before it submits its server for the check (document 05, section 5.6), a new
  super-node takes from the other holders every stored announcement of the kinds it will hold — by Negentropy set reconciliation (NIP-77)
  where the other relay supports it, so that only the missing events travel — checks the signatures and builds its index; it reads
  receipts and reviews from the blockchain. A super-node coming back after downtime does the same from the moment it last saw (the
  `since` filter of NIP-01). It copies signed announcements, never another super-node's index or result list, so it has to trust
  nobody: an announcement that was forged or altered fails its signature.
- **The index is checked.** The checks by agents in turn — at entry and for the quality minimum of every period — include the index: an
  announcement that has been on the relays of the other holders for longer than the propagation time must appear in this super-node's
  results when it matches the query and lies within its coverage. A super-node whose index misses such announcements fails the check; as
  with downtime, it loses income and, if it keeps failing, its place, without a mark. Dropping one agent inside a declared kind remains a
  violation (section 17.3).
- **Announcements expire.** Every announcement carries an expiration (NIP-40) no further ahead than a fixed period; a node renews its
  announcements while its agents work, and relays and indexes drop expired ones. Storage therefore follows the active agents and their
  services — one latest version for each «agent key + kind + `d` tag» (NIP-01) — not the history of updates and not agents that have
  left.

**Why.** Discovery is one of the network's two goals (entry 20), and it cannot depend on which relays an agent happened to know. With the
relay address in the contract and the holders computed from it, every node and every newcomer finds the right relays without any central
list, so no single point of failure appears. A full copy of every announcement on every super-node, copied from every other super-node,
would make each super-node's work grow with the whole network — exactly what entry 47 forbids; holders keep that work bounded, and the
search fee spreads the busy kinds. A search for one kind is answered by one holder, which keeps the whole kind, so the ranking of section
17.2 and the turn of section 17.3 stay as they are. «I never received it» is no longer an answer: an announcement on the other holders'
relays is expected in every index that holds its kind. The cost is stated: a node publishes each update to at least k super-nodes; a
holder keeps a subscription to the other holders of each of its kinds; a newcomer's catch-up grows with the size of the kinds it takes on.
The constant k, the propagation time, the longest expiration and what happens to a kind too large for one server are open (open
questions).

**Documents:** 05, 06, 15, 17, 18, 19; README; READMEs of `lagrix-node`, `lagrix-supernode` and `lagrix-contracts`; lagrix.dev.

## 49. Official agents: the Official mark, decided by a random panel of super-nodes

*Agreed on 17 October. New. Revises entries 1, 24 and 27 for this one procedure: there is still no council and no standing body, and the
network still does not judge services.*

**Before.** The network saw keys, not people (entry 27). Anyone could publish an agent under any name — a famous person's or a
company's — and nothing helped a counterparty tell the real agent from a copy. There was no vote of any kind (entries 1 and 24).

**Now.**
- **The Official mark.** A node may apply for the mark «Official» for a person or an organisation it represents. The mark stands on the
  node's wallet and on all its elements and shows the name, what the person or organisation is known for, the sources and the date.
  There is one mark per person or organisation, not per name: namesakes are told apart by what each is known for.
- **What the applicant presents.** At least three official sources that have already verified this person or organisation — accounts
  on platforms that have themselves confirmed whose they are — each with a post that carries the node's wallet address. The applicant's
  own domain is not a source. The posts stay published for as long as the mark lives.
- **Who decides.** Nine super-nodes chosen at random among those that passed the quality minimum in the period, with commit and reveal
  as for places (entry 31). Each member decides by its own judgment which sources to trust: no rule lists platforms, and no machine
  approves or refuses. Votes stay hidden until all are revealed and are public afterwards. The mark is given when at least eight of the
  nine vote yes.
- **The fee.** $100 in USDC, paid with the application and not returned whatever the outcome. It is divided equally among the panel
  members who voted; a member that does not vote receives nothing.
- **A challenge.** Anyone may challenge a mark with an application of their own, the same fee and their own three sources. A new panel
  decides; if at least eight of the nine find for the challenger, the mark moves to the challenger's wallet. A deleted source is a ground
  for a challenge.
- **What the loser loses.** A refused applicant loses its fee; a holder that loses a challenge loses the mark. No other mark is added.
- **The start.** The procedure runs once ten super-nodes have passed the quality minimum in a period (entries 40 and 41). Until then the
  only mark is the founder's.
- **The founder's mark.** The contracts carry one mark from deployment: the founder's name as the founder is publicly known, the wallet
  address of the founder's node (entry 41) and two sources — github.com/bolshiyanov and lagrix.dev. No documents are written. Once the
  procedure runs, this mark can be challenged like any other; that is also how the founder would recover it if the key were stolen.
- **What the mark does not do.** It does not move an agent in search results (document 17, sections 17.2 and 17.7), opens no
  conversation without its owner's yes (entry 11) and changes no rule, fee or payment.

**Why.**
- Discovery promises a direct line to anyone through their agent (entry 20). If an impostor's agent cannot be told from the real one,
  that line becomes a channel for fraud: in six months the US Federal Trade Commission counted more than $2 million sent to impostors of
  a single well-known entrepreneur (Data Spotlight, May 2021).
- Whom the public means by a name cannot be computed; it is a judgment. Platforms that have already verified a person have done most of
  that work, and three such sources mean that one taken-over account is not enough to take the mark.
- A panel of nine chosen at random for each application is not a standing body: it decides one application and dissolves, and nobody
  knows its members in advance. A fee kept whatever the outcome gives the panel no gain from refusing, and eight of nine keep one or two
  careless or bribed votes from deciding.
- The founder's mark exists because the procedure cannot run before ten super-nodes pass the quality minimum, while people need to
  recognise the author of the protocol from the first day. It carries only what is already public about the founder and can be
  challenged like any other.
- **The cost we do not hide.** A panel can be deceived or bribed, and votes made public after the reveal can be checked by whoever paid
  for them. A mark ties the whole history of a wallet to a person or an organisation, so an official agent is best run on a node of its
  own. Until ten super-nodes pass the quality minimum, nobody but the founder can carry the mark.

**Documents:** 24 (new), 05, 17, 18, 22, README; READMEs of `lagrix-supernode` and `lagrix-contracts`.

## 50. Review pages: a review may link to a page its author published

*Agreed on 17 October. New. Extends entries 26 and 43: a review is still a like or a dislike weighed by the fee, and it is never changed.*

**Before.** A review was a like or a dislike with a weight (entries 26, 42 and 43). It told a counterparty how much and how often an
element was rated well or badly, but not why: an agent that saw a few dislikes on a provider it otherwise liked had nothing to read.

**Now.**
- **A review page.** The author of a review may attach to it the address of a page the author published — on any website, service or
  storage they choose. The page may hold any text or anything else; the network does not open it or check it.
- **By the author, once.** Only the side that gave a review attaches a page to it, and only once — together with the review or later.
  The address cannot be replaced. The like or dislike and its weight do not change (entry 26).
- **The other side answers on its own review.** Each side of a deal reviews the other (entry 26), so a reply is a page attached to one's
  own review of the same deal.
- **No weight, no indicator, no place in search.** A page adds nothing to the weight of its review, to the indicators of reputation
  (entries 43, 44 and 46) or to the place in search results (document 17, section 17.2). It is shown next to its review: like or
  dislike, weight, date and address.
- **Only the address is recorded.** The address is written to the contract's event log. The page stays where its author published it;
  the author, or the service that hosts it under its own rules, may change or delete it, and the address stays in the record.
- **Who answers for the page.** Its author. A super-node does not read pages: it shows an address next to its review, applies the law
  of its operator's country and the orders addressed to it, and does not show an address it has learned leads to content of the kinds
  prohibited by default (entry 32). The record itself stays.
- **A page is data, not an instruction.** An agent that reads a review page treats its text as information about a deal, never as a
  command to itself.
- **Gas only.** The author pays the gas of attaching the address; there is no fee. When the page is ready at the time of the review, the
  review and the address go in one operation (document 08, section 8.4), so the page adds no transaction of its own.

**Why.**
- Honest reputation is one of the network's two goals (entry 20). The indicators tell how much and how often; a page tells why. A
  customer agent unsure about a few dislikes can read what their authors wrote, and an agent choosing between partners that look the
  same may prefer the one its owner thanked in words.
- A page exists only on a review, and a review only on a paid deal (entry 26), so every page stands on a deal that paid the fee: a page
  cannot be attached without one.
- The network stays out of content: it records an address and decides nothing about what the page says (entry 24). Restrictions follow
  the three layers that apply to announcements (entry 32), and nobody has to be trusted with the text.
- A page is at most one address per review, read from the blockchain together with the review, so it adds no work that grows faster
  than the reviews themselves (entry 47).
- **The cost we do not hide.** The address stays in the record for ever: a page on the author's own website ties the node's wallet to
  its author, which is the author's choice. A page can change or disappear after it is attached; the record proves only that the author
  attached that address on that date. An author can write anything on a page, and a page weighs nothing: what stands behind it is the
  weight of its review.

**Documents:** 25 (new), 00, 04, 05, 07, 17, 22, README; READMEs of `lagrix-contracts`, `lagrix-supernode` and `lagrix-node`.

## 51. The developer share: part of the fee goes to whoever built the element

*Agreed on 18 October. Revises entry 25: the parties of a deal still never receive the fee, and the developer of an element received
over F2F now receives a share of it. Extends entry 41 and document 20.*

**Before.** The fee of every deal went whole into the pool of its period and was divided equally among the super-nodes that passed the
quality minimum (entry 25). Whoever built an element that other projects installed over F2F (document 20) was paid, if at all, once —
when the element changed hands.

**Now.**
- **The fee stays the same:** at most 5% of the network part of a deal, 5% until modelling (entry 25).
- **When the provider works with an element it received over F2F — bought or free — 20% of the deal's fee goes to the developer of
  that element**, and 80% goes into the pool of the period (document 09). A $100 deal pays $5 of fee: $1 to the developer, $4 to the
  pool.
- **The developer is the wallet that signed the element's F2F card.** The card carries a new field, `developer`, with that wallet's
  address (document 20). The provider's node names the developer when it records its result in the contract (`commitResult`,
  document 04, section 4.3); the escrow contract pays the share when the deal moves to COMPLETED. A deal that ends in a refund pays no fee and so no share.
- **The provider's own element** — one it did not receive over F2F — pays the whole fee into the pool.
- **The weight of a review does not change:** it is the whole fee paid on the deal (entry 42).
- **The founder takes no developer share.** To the commitments of entry 41 one is added: no developer share is taken by the founder's
  named node; it stays in the pool. Like entry 41, this is a commitment of the founder as a person, not a rule of the contracts.
- **20% is the starting share.** Whether it should depend on the reputation of the customer agent is open.

**Why.**
- Discovery promises an agent for anything (entry 20), and there are agents for anything only if people build them. Whoever builds an
  element that lets a person earn — a driver, a tutor, a repairer — is paid from the network's part for as long as the element works,
  not from the provider's pay.
- The share comes out of the fee the parties already pay: a deal costs the customer and the provider exactly what it cost before.
- A developer is paid for the code it wrote, not for holding a node. Entry 25 refuses to pay the nodes of agents, because nodes are cheap
  to multiply; the developer share is paid only for an element that another project installed over F2F.
- **The cost we do not hide.** The contracts cannot tell an element received over F2F from a node's own: they see only the
  `developer` wallet the provider names. A node that makes deals with itself and, as provider, names a wallet of its own as the developer
  gets 20% of the fee back: a unit of review weight then costs it 80 cents, not a dollar. The weight stays the whole fee by choice — one
  rule for every deal — and such deals are visible in the chain: the same `developer` wallet on deals between the same nodes. Nor can
  the contracts check that the code a provider runs is the code its card describes, so a provider could name a developer that did not
  build its element — a wallet of its own included, keeping a fifth of the fee on its deals with others too.

**Documents:** 26 (new), 04, 05, 07, 09, 17, 20, 22, README; README of `lagrix-contracts`.

## 52. Messages: one voucher with a running total, only text through super-nodes, attachments stay with the sender, a first-contact rate paid on reading

*Agreed on 18 October. Revises entries 5, 19, 33 and 39 as far as vouchers, delivery and storage go, and turns the first-contact rate of
document 23 into a rule.*

**Before.** A searcher signed a voucher for each search and a sender a voucher for each delivered message, and a super-node redeemed
every voucher in a batch, each with its own signature and nonce (entries 5, 19 and 33; document 17, section 17.8). A delivered message
cost $0.001 whatever its size, and a super-node held messages for an offline recipient with no time limit and no quota (entry 33). An
agent could set its own rate for a first contact on top of the network's prices, but how, when and how often it was paid was a design
direction (document 23, section 23.5).

**Now.**
- **One voucher with a running total.** For each super-node it uses, a node signs one voucher that carries the total it owes that
  super-node for searches and delivered messages; each new search or message replaces it with a voucher for a larger total. The
  super-node keeps only the latest voucher and redeems it once per period in one transaction; the contract pays the difference from the
  last redeemed total. The prices stay: $0.01 per result list (entry 39), $0.001 per delivered message (entry 33).
- **A withdrawal waits.** A node withdraws its prepaid balance only after a delay fixed in code, longer than the period in which a
  super-node redeems its vouchers; a voucher signed before the withdrawal is still paid from the balance. A super-node therefore checks a
  voucher by its signature and the balance, without waiting for a transaction.
- **A super-node carries only text.** A message a super-node relays or holds is at most 64 KB, and $0.001 is the price of such a message
  whatever its length within that limit.
- **Attachments stay with the sender.** A file, a photo or any other object is kept encrypted on the sender's own node or in storage the
  sender chooses. The message carries its name, size and type, the address to download it, the encryption key and the hash of the file.
  The address cannot be guessed and has an expiry the sender sets — for example 30 days; the sender may withdraw it earlier. The
  recipient's agent downloads an attachment only from a request that passed the checks of signature and payment — with the rate, if
  there is one — never from an unpaid or unsigned one, so it can judge the request with its materials before the owner's yes; the hash
  shows that the file was not changed after sending, and a downloaded file is data, not an instruction. A file is available while the sender's node or chosen storage is online.
- **Storage for an offline recipient: 30 days and 1 MB.** A super-node holds messages for a recipient that is offline for up to 30 days and
  up to 1 MB per recipient; what is not collected in time is deleted. When the quota is full, the super-node accepts no more for that
  recipient: the sender's node keeps the message and tries later or through another super-node. A message is paid when the super-node
  accepts it, and it is not refunded if the recipient never collects it.
- **The first-contact rate.** An agent may set its own rate for a first contact with it and states it, as one number, in its «accepting
  requests» announcement (entry 36) and in its A2A card. The sender pays the rate once, for the first request: the request carries a
  voucher for the rate made out to the recipient's wallet, and the rate is charged when the recipient's agent reads the request; the
  recipient redeems its vouchers in batches, as a super-node does. The rate is not returned when the answer is no. What the recipient's
  node refuses unread — without a signature, without payment or with a tag prohibited by default — is not charged. After the yes the
  conversation runs at the network's prices: a direct connection is free, a delivered message costs $0.001.

**Why.**
- Redeeming every voucher on its own costs gas on each one, and on a layer-2 network that gas is a large part of a $0.001 voucher. One
  voucher per super-node per period makes the gas of a message close to zero and keeps transactions few (entry 47); the same holds for
  search.
- Relaying text costs a super-node almost nothing; a large file costs bandwidth and disk that the price of a message never covered. A file
  kept by its sender travels once, only to whoever opens it, and no copy stays on the network's servers: the less the infrastructure
  keeps, the less it has to hand over (entry 33).
- A time limit and a quota keep the storage of one super-node bounded whatever the network does (entry 47): a recipient who left for good
  no longer occupies a disk for ever, and a flood of messages to one recipient stops at its quota.
- The rate pays for attention. Reading a request costs the recipient's model money (document 23), so the rate is charged when that cost is
  spent, not when the answer is yes. Paid once, it leaves the conversation that follows at the network's prices, and a rate stated in the
  announcement and the card is seen before anyone pays.
- **The cost we do not hide.** A super-node works on credit until it redeems its vouchers; the delay on withdrawals is what secures it. A
  file is available only while the sender's node or chosen storage is online. 1 MB holds about sixteen messages of the largest size, so a
  sender to a recipient long offline may have to wait or try another super-node. The sender cannot prove that its request was read: a
  node that charged rates without reading would show only in the requests it leaves unanswered.

## 53. Two deadlines in every deal: instant and deferred deals, long work as a series

*Agreed on 18 October. Revises entry 24 as far as the acceptance window goes, and document 04 (section 4.3): the dispute window is no
longer one constant for the whole network. Revised by entry 54: there is no «missed orders» indicator, and an order confirmation stays
between the agents.*

**Before.** The escrow contract had one dispute window for every deal — a constant in code, for example 5 minutes (`DISPUTE_PERIOD`,
document 04). A deal had no delivery deadline of its own: document 04 returned the payment to the customer when the provider «did not
deliver by the deadline», but no deal recorded that deadline and no function let the customer take its money back; the SDK example
waited 300 seconds for a result. Every deal was built as one that closes minutes after it is paid — a model's answer, a file. A haircut
booked for the day after tomorrow, a delivery, or care that lasts three months did not fit.

**Now.**
- **Every deal carries two deadlines.** The customer sets them when it locks the payment (`lockFunds`), and both are written into the
  deal:
  - **the delivery deadline** (`deliverBy`) — the moment by which the provider must record delivery (`commitResult`); a delivery
    recorded later is rejected;
  - **the dispute window** (`disputeWindow`) — how long the customer has after delivery to accept the work or cancel the order; when it
    passes in silence, the provider closes the deal (`claimTimeout`), as before.
- **Limits fixed in code:** the delivery deadline is at most 90 days after the lock, the dispute window at most 14 days, so a deal never
  keeps money locked longer than 104 days. A limit changes only with a new version of the contracts (entry 1).
- **A missed deadline returns the money.** If the delivery deadline passes with no delivery, the customer takes back the whole network
  part (`claimRefund`): the deal moves to REFUNDED, no fee is taken and no receipt is written. Before delivery the provider may decline
  the task at any time (`declineTask`), with the same result.
- **Two kinds of deal on one set of states.** LOCKED → COMMITTED → COMPLETED, REFUNDED or CANCELLED stay as they are; the kinds differ
  only in their deadlines:
  - **an instant deal** — the result is data handed over at delivery and checked by the customer's agent itself: an answer, a file, a
    digital product; both deadlines are minutes;
  - **a deferred deal** — the work happens in the world or on a set date, and the person checks it through their own agent: a haircut,
    a delivery, a repair, a lesson; the delivery deadline is the agreed time with a margin, the dispute window is hours or days.
  The contract does not store the kind — it sees two numbers. The kind is a word for people and a tag in the announcement.
- **The provider states its terms in advance.** An announcement carries the kind of the service and its dispute window (document 17,
  tag `deal`); an announcement without the tag offers instant deals. The provider sees both deadlines of a deal before it starts work
  and declines a deal whose deadlines it did not agree to.
- **Cancelling before the work starts needs nothing new:** the customer asks, and the provider declines the task — the whole network
  part returns. If the provider does not agree, the customer may cancel after delivery, within the dispute window, and gets back at
  most the weight of its likes (entry 42).
- **Long work is a series of deferred deals, one per period** — a week or a month. The customer's agent locks the payment for a period
  before it starts, and the provider does not start a period that is not locked in escrow. Each period is an ordinary deal with its own
  receipt and reviews, and either side may stop after any period. The contracts do not know about a series; the agents of both sides
  link its deals on their own nodes.
- **The fee goes into the pool of the period in which the deal closes**, however long ago it was locked (document 09).
- Document 27 describes the whole life of a deal in one place; document 04 keeps its mechanics.

**Why.**
- One constant cannot serve both a model's answer and a haircut: five minutes after a haircut the customer has barely left the chair,
  and a window of days would hold a provider of instant answers without pay for days. Deadlines in the deal give each service the time it
  really needs.
- Without a delivery deadline in the deal, a customer whose provider never delivered had no way back to its money: the deal could stay
  open for ever. The deadline closes every deal — by delivery and the dispute window, or by a refund.
- Two kinds on one set of states keep the contract small: auditors check one machine, and nothing can break between stages. A process
  of many stages — milestones inside one deal — would make the escrow a judge of stages, which the network refuses to be (entry 24).
- A series puts at risk one period on each side, not three months; each period writes its receipt, so reputation grows with the work,
  not at its end. This is payment on completion for long work without locking months of money.
- The limits keep money from being frozen by a mistake: a deadline set years ahead would lock the customer's payment for years.
- **The cost we do not hide.** A provider that took an order and did not come loses only that deal: the money returns, and its
  reputation shows nothing. Counting missed orders would need a step in which the provider confirms the order — without it, anyone could
  damage a provider's reputation by locking deals it never saw; that step is open. A series of thirteen weekly deals counts as thirteen
  orders in «all orders», though the sums are exact. A deferred deal keeps the customer's money locked for days or weeks, and the
  provider still works before it is paid.

**Documents:** 27 (new), 00, 04, 07, 12, 13, 17, 21, 22, README; READMEs of `lagrix-contracts` and `lagrix-node`; lagrix.dev.

## 54. No «missed orders»; an order confirmation stays between the agents

*Agreed on 18 October. Answers the open question of entry 53 on confirming an order and missed orders. Revised by entry 55: a
cancelled order gives the customer a review to answer a false delivery with.*

**Before.** Entry 53 left open whether a provider confirms a deferred order before its date, and whether orders it confirmed and did not
deliver show in its reputation as «missed orders».

**Now.**
- **Reputation has no «missed orders» indicator.** A deal that ends because the provider declined it or let the delivery deadline pass
  returns the whole network part to the customer (entry 53) and leaves no mark on either side.
- **An order confirmation is an agreement between the agents, not a rule of the network.** A provider's agent may confirm a deferred
  order to the customer's agent — for example with an off-chain signature of the order and its date, like the acceptance signature
  (document 04, section 4.2) — so that the customer knows its time is held. The contracts do not read it, and it changes neither the deal
  nor anyone's reputation.

**Why.**
- A provider that did not come has two ways out. If it lets the delivery deadline pass, the customer takes the whole payment back. If it
  records a false delivery, the customer can only cancel within the dispute window and gets back at most the weight of its likes; the rest
  goes to the provider. A $40 haircut and a customer with $3 of likes: a false delivery brings the provider about $37, an honest miss
  brings nothing.
- A «missed order» would therefore be recorded only for a provider that admitted it had failed; one that lied would never get it. The
  indicator would teach providers to lie, and reputation exists to be honest (entry 20).
- A provider that records false deliveries leaves another trace: cancelled orders in its role as provider (entries 42 and 43).
- **The cost we do not hide.** While the customer has few likes, a false delivery stays profitable for a dishonest provider: the weight of
  the customer's likes is all that protects it. Whether a cancelled order lets the customer answer with a review is open (entry 42).

**Documents:** 27; lagrix.dev.

## 55. A cancelled order: the fee on the provider's part, reviews from both sides, no receipt

*Agreed on 18 October. Answers the open question of entry 42 on a cancelled order; extends entry 54.*

**Before.** A customer that cancelled an order within the dispute window got back at most the weight of its likes, and the provider
received the rest (entries 42 and 46). Whether the fee was taken from the provider's part, and whether a cancelled order left a receipt
and reviews, was not decided. A customer cheated by a false delivery (entry 54) could cancel, but had no review to answer with.

**Now.**
- **The fee is taken from the part the provider receives** — at the same rate as on any deal, at most 5% — and is divided as usual: into
  the pool of the period in which the order was cancelled, less the developer share when the provider works with an element received
  over F2F (entries 25 and 51).
- **Both sides may review a cancelled order:** the customer the provider, and the provider the customer, one like or dislike each, as
  after a completed deal (entry 26). Each review weighs the fee paid on that order. A cancelled order with a fee counts in the reviewable
  weight that negative ratings are read against, and in «unreviewed» until its side gives a review (entries 43 and 46).
- **A refund of the whole network part takes no fee and gives no review:** nothing was paid to the provider, so there is nothing to
  weigh.
- **A cancelled order writes no receipt.** It does not count as paid work for search results or for a super-node place, and it does not
  add to the number of closed deals; it shows in «all orders» and «cancelled orders», as before (entry 44).
- Example: a $40 haircut and a customer with $3 of likes. The customer gets $3 back; of the $37 left, the fee is $1.85 and the provider
  receives $35.15; each side's review weighs $1.85.

**Why.**
- A customer cheated by a false delivery gets a voice with real weight, and the next customer sees it. The review does not return the
  money; it warns the others.
- An honest provider stays protected: to leave it a dislike of $1.85, a demanding customer first pays it $37 and loses $3 of its own
  likes. Weight is never had for less than it weighs, and harming a reputation still costs more than the harm (document 17, section 17.5).
- The fee is what gives a review its weight: without it, the review of a cancelled order would weigh nothing.
- A receipt would let a false delivery lift a dishonest provider in search — it would gain both the money and a place. Search follows
  work that was paid and accepted.
- **The cost we do not hide.** A cancelled order now costs the provider the fee on its part. And a review weighs only the fee on what the
  provider kept, so a customer with many likes, refunded almost in full, leaves a light review.

**Documents:** 04, 07, 09, 17, 26, 27, README; README of `lagrix-contracts`; lagrix.dev.

## Contradictions resolved

- **The delivery deadline and the dispute window** (document 04, README glossary, lagrix.dev). The words «acceptance window» named two
  different deadlines: in document 04 the time by which the provider must deliver (no delivery — the money returns to the customer), in
  the glossary the time in which the customer must answer after delivery (no answer — the money goes to the provider). Now the first is
  the «delivery deadline», the second the «dispute window», and «acceptance» remains the customer's act.
- **Downtime is not penalised** (document 06). Document 16 described downtime as leading to `slashValidator()` and "Jail"; it now
  follows 06.
- **The network does not depend on our domain.** `paymaster.lagrix.dev` (documents 12, 13) and `get.lagrix.dev` (document 15) are
  removed: the paymaster is a contract address, and the operator's tools come from the repository's releases.
- **Discovery runs through Nostr and the super-node's index** (document 17). Documents 12 and 13 described a separate Kademlia service
  registry; they now follow 17. The SDK remembers a provider it has found and does not search again for every task.
- **A vacancy reopens on the terms of the day it reopens** (entries 15, 16). Documents 05 and 06 said that a vacated place
  reopens on the terms on which it was taken; they now follow this changelog.
- **An agent is found by its announcement, not in the DHT** (documents 01, 02, 03, 14; 18 October). These documents described agents
  storing their address and encryption key in the Kademlia DHT and clients looking them up there. An agent's address, card and key travel
  in its signed announcement (document 17, section 17.1); the DHT is the super-nodes' routing table (document 18, section 18.1), and agents
  behind a router exchange their public addresses at the rendezvous through a super-node (document 02).
- **No period reward for relaying** (document 02; 18 October). A sentence from before entry 42 paid a super-node «a share of every
  period's reward»; there is no such reward. A super-node is paid its share of the fee pool and the search and delivery fees; a delivered
  H2H message costs $0.001 (entry 33).
- **Availability is measured by agents in turn** (documents 06, 14, 16; 18 October). Neighbouring super-nodes measured availability by
  PING; competitors do not judge each other (document 05, section 5.6), so availability is measured by the checks of agents taken in turn
  (entry 30), and the Kademlia PING only keeps routing tables fresh.
- **One wallet per node** (documents 03, 08; 18 October). These documents spoke of each agent's own wallet or smart account and of a NodeID
  «declared in the escrow contract»; a node has one wallet for all its elements and agents (entries 22 and 39), agents get session keys of
  its smart account, and the escrow deal records the wallets of the two sides (document 04).
- **Cancelled orders in the SDK** (document 12; 18 October). The SDK listed no CANCELLED state, and its cancellation returned REFUNDED. A
  customer's cancellation within the dispute window ends CANCELLED with a refund of at most the weight of its likes; REFUNDED is a declined
  or undelivered task (document 04).
- **Envoy is the reference implementation** (documents 01, 03, 12; 18 October). Envoy was described as a sidecar every agent must run; any
  program that gives the encrypted channel of document 19 is a node.
- **A super-node's gas** (document 16; 18 October). An alert spoke of gas «for serving UserOps» of a bundler; a super-node pays gas only for
  its own transactions (entry 38).
- **Offline recipients of H2H** (document 21; 18 October). «Both sides must be online» stood among the limits of document 21; a super-node
  holds an encrypted message for an offline recipient for $0.001 (entry 33, step 4 of the same document).
- **The list of contracts** (document 07; 18 October). OfficialMarks.sol (entry 49) and the delivery vouchers of SearchVouchers.sol
  (entry 33) were missing.
- **Who names the developer** (entry 51, documents 04, 07, 26; 18 October). Entry 51 had the provider's node name the developer «when the
  deal is created», but the customer creates the deal; the provider names it when it records its result (`commitResult`), and the deal
  and its receipt carry the field `developer`. The cost of entry 51 is stated in full: the contracts cannot tell an element received over
  F2F from a node's own, so a node that names a wallet of its own as the developer keeps a fifth of the fee (documents 05, 09, 17, 22, 26,
  README).
- **Smaller wording** (documents 00, 07, 17, 18, 20; 18 October): the fee is described with the developer share; «access credentials» and
  «USDC transfers» replace the word «tokens»; under overload two places open and then the worst super-node leaves (entry 40).
- **The fee split, one reading** (README, documents 00, 05, 09, 22, 27; README of `lagrix-supernode`; lagrix.dev; 18 October). Some
  sentences sent the whole fee to the super-nodes without the developer share, others gave the share only as «20% of the fee», and a few
  said a unit of review weight always costs a dollar. Entry 51 is unchanged; every place that says where a deal's fee goes now names
  both cases at the level of the deal: at a 5% fee, an element received over F2F gives 1% of the deal to its developer and 4% to the pool,
  the provider's own element gives all 5% to the pool; the 80-cent exception of entry 51 is named wherever weight is said to cost a
  dollar. What a super-node is paid for — the pool, the redistribution of the shares of those that fail the minimum, search, delivery, the
  Official panel fee and the reward for proving a violation — is listed once, in document 05, section 5.7.

## Open questions

These are not decided in this revision and are marked where they appear. The entry of super-nodes beyond the first 100 and the
live-agent check, open in the first part of this revision, are answered by entries 15 and 16.

- **How "passed or failed" is measured.** Entry 30 says agents taken in turn check each super-node against a quality minimum;
  what they measure, how the turn is kept and how their results are combined is not decided. The same holds for the overload of the
  network and for the checks under load that decide which super-node leaves (entry 40), and for the capacity warning: who sends it, what «short»
  means and the deadline (entry 45), and for the check of the index (entry 48).
- **The `superNode` field of a deal.** The customer names the super-node that receives a deal's receipt (document 04); nothing yet ties
  it to the node that actually served the deal.
- **Payment for relaying traffic.** Earlier documents disagreed — in USDC per megabyte or none at all. For H2H messages it is
  decided by entries 33 and 52 ($0.001 per delivered message of up to 64 KB; attachments stay with the sender); other relayed traffic is
  still described without a price.
- **The time slot of the search turn** (entry 30): its length is set by modelling.
- **The holders of a kind and the life of an announcement** (entry 48): the constant k, how long an announcement may take to reach the
  other holders before its absence counts against an index, how far ahead an expiration may be set, how the key of a kind is computed,
  and what happens to a kind too large for one server, are set by modelling and at implementation.
- **The thresholds of overload** (entry 47): the constants of deals, redeemed searches and delivered messages per super-node above which
  new places open are set by modelling.
- **How the contract finds the median cheaply** (entry 31): recomputing over all nodes for every open place is expensive; the method is
  not chosen.
- **Collusion at reveal** (entry 31): the last revealer can withhold its secret and so change the result — it cannot help itself this
  way, but it can help an accomplice. How this is penalised is not decided.
- **The names of layer 1 tags and the format of a signed restriction list** (entry 32): chosen at implementation.
- **The reward to whoever proves a violation** (entry 42): its size, paid in USDC from the fees, is set by modelling.
- **Whether the fees pay for super-node servers while the network is small** (entry 42): checked by modelling.
- **The Official mark** (entry 49): how long the commit and reveal windows last, how often a mark may be challenged, whether a
  panel member that does not vote is replaced, and whether a holder may move its mark to a new wallet of its own without a challenge.
- **The review page** (entry 50): the longest address a page may have is chosen at implementation.
- **The developer share** (entry 51): whether the share depends on the reputation of the customer agent; how a receiving project
  checks that the code it installs matches the card; who is the developer of an element changed after it was installed.
- **The voucher with a running total** (entry 52): the length of the redemption period and of the withdrawal delay are set by modelling.
- **The first-contact rate** (entry 52): whether a rate may depend on who writes; whether the recipient may give a rate back.
- **A series in reputation** (entry 53): whether the deals of one series are shown as one line is not decided.

en.title: 1. Network Topology: Kademlia DHT, Node ID and Routing Algorithms
en.text:
# 1. Network Topology: Kademlia DHT, Node ID and Routing Algorithms

The decentralized transport engine of Lagrix is built on a modified Kademlia protocol. The standard Kademlia implementation is vulnerable to Sybil attacks, so our architecture rigidly binds P2P identifiers to registered super-node places. A place is earned by a year of paid work, which creates a real barrier to entering the routing table.

## 1.1 Node ID Generation and Crypto-Economic Binding

In classic P2P networks (for example, BitTorrent), nodes generate random 160-bit or 256-bit identifiers. In Lagrix this is strictly forbidden.

The Super-Node identifier (NodeID) is deterministically computed from the public key of the wallet (Ethereum/EVM-compatible) from which the place was registered in the SuperNodeRegistry.sol smart contract.

Formula: $NodeID = \text{SHA3-256}(PublicKey_{EVM})$

Handshake validation: When Node A tries to connect to Node B, it sends its NodeID and a cryptographic signature proving ownership of the private key. Node B takes the public key, queries a blockchain RPC node and checks that this address is an active super-node — it has entered under document 05, section 5.6 (a place assigned by random choice and registered on-chain) and carries no «proven violation» mark (document 06): `isActiveSuperNode(PublicKey) == true`.

Result: If the address is not an active super-node, the connection is dropped instantly at the socket level. An attacker cannot fill the network with a million fake NodeIDs, because each one requires a real entry: a place assigned by random choice among owners of provider agents with a year of paid work, and a server that passed the check.

## 1.2 Routing Mathematics (XOR Metric)

Routing between super-nodes relies on computing the logical exclusive OR (XOR) between identifiers. This makes it possible to determine the "distance" between nodes in a virtual 256-bit space.

Distance: $d(x, y) = x \oplus y$

Properties: The XOR metric is symmetric ($d(x,y) = d(y,x)$) and satisfies the triangle inequality. This means that a lookup among super-nodes always converges in logarithmic time $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$, where $N$ is the number of Super-Nodes in the network.

In practice: If a super-node needs to find the node with ID 0xABCD..., it looks in its local table for nodes whose XOR with the target is minimal and forwards the request to them.

## 1.3 Routing Tables (K-Buckets)

Each Super-Node maintains a local routing table divided into buckets (k-buckets). In a 256-bit space there are 256 buckets.

Parameter $k$: Each bucket stores at most $k=20$ active nodes. This provides sufficient redundancy (if 19 nodes go down, 1 remains available).

Eviction policy: Kademlia gives preference to "old" nodes. If a bucket is full, the new node is placed in a waiting buffer. A PING is sent to the existing nodes. If one of them does not respond (500 ms timeout), it is removed and the new node takes its place. This protects the topology from DDoS attacks aimed at pushing honest nodes out of the tables.

## 1.4 P2P Message Lifecycle (RPC Methods)

Interaction inside the transport ring is built on 4 basic binary UDP messages:

| RPC Method | Purpose in the Lagrix architecture |
|---|---|
| PING | Checks that a node is alive. Used to keep k-buckets up to date. |
| STORE | Writes a record on the $k$ closest super-nodes — records of the super-nodes' own routing. An agent's address, card and encryption key are not stored in the DHT: they travel in its signed announcement (document 17, section 17.1). |
| FIND_NODE | Requests a list of $k$ nodes closest to the target ID. Used to build the network map. |
| FIND_VALUE | Reads such a record. An agent is found by its announcement and the super-nodes' index, not by the DHT (document 17). |

## 1.5 Integration with the Local Data Plane (Envoy)

In the reference implementation the Kademlia module and the client's discovery code play the role of the Control Plane. It does not move the actual gigabytes of data between AI agents.

As soon as the client knows the target agent's address — from its announcement (document 17) and, behind a router, from the rendezvous through a super-node (document 02) — this information is instantly passed over a local gRPC channel (xDS API) to Envoy Proxy, which then opens a high-speed mTLS tunnel to transfer the payload. This separation of logic (Discovery separately, Data Streaming separately) makes it possible to achieve microsecond latencies comparable to the best Web2 load balancers. A node may use any other transport that gives the encrypted channel of document 19.

en.title: 2. P2P & NAT Traversal: Breaking Through Firewalls and Relay Bridges
en.text:
# 2. P2P & NAT Traversal: Breaking Through Firewalls and Relay Bridges

Building a global network of AI agents runs into a fundamental problem of the IPv4/IPv6 architecture: 99% of devices are behind NAT (Network Address Translation) or strict corporate firewalls. Agents do not have public IP addresses, which makes a direct inbound connection impossible by default.

Lagrix implements a custom ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) stack integrated with the protocol's super-nodes.

## 2.1 Anatomy of the Problem and Node Roles in NAT Traversal

In classic Web2 this problem is solved with centralized STUN/TURN servers from Google or Twilio. In our architecture this role is taken over by decentralized Super-Nodes (Core Relays), which have dedicated "white" (public) IP addresses, and their operators maintain the infrastructure.

NAT types the protocol works with:

Full Cone / Restricted Cone NAT (home networks): Allow UDP Hole Punching.

Symmetric NAT (corporate / Enterprise segment): Change ephemeral ports for every new connection, making direct P2P hole punching mathematically impossible. Require a Relay fallback.

## 2.2 Phase 1: STUN Identification (Endpoint Discovery)

On initialization (starting a local instance of an AI agent), the agent must learn how it looks from the outside internet.

Binding Request: The client agent (Edge Node) sends a STUN_BINDING UDP packet to three Super-Nodes it knows.

Mapping Response: The Super-Node reads the packet's IP header and answers the agent: "I see your traffic from IP 203.0.113.5, port 45123".

Handing over the address: The agent keeps this pair (Public IP : Port), signed with its private session key, and gives it to the other side at the rendezvous through a super-node (section 2.3). It does not publish it: the agent itself is found by its signed announcement, which carries its node, card and encryption key (document 17, section 17.1).

## 2.3 Phase 2: UDP Hole Punching Mechanics (Direct Connection)

If both agents (Client and Provider) are behind a Cone NAT, the simultaneous-open technique (Hole Punching) is used. This is the fastest and free (in terms of gas) way to communicate.

Initiation: Agent A (Client) wants to send a prompt to Agent B (Provider). Agent A has found B by its announcement (document 17).

Synchronization (Rendezvous): Through a Super-Node, the two agents exchange their public addresses (section 2.2), and Agent A tells Agent B: "I am about to start sending you packets, open your port".

Simultaneous punch:

Agent A sends a UDP packet to B's public address. Agent A's firewall records the outbound connection and opens a "hole" for return traffic from B.

At the same time Agent B sends a UDP packet to A's public address. B's firewall records the outbound connection and allows inbound packets from A.

Result: The packets cross in the providers' routers. A direct, microsecond P2P channel is formed. The Super-Nodes no longer take part in the transfer, saving bandwidth.

## 2.4 Phase 3: Relay Fallback (TURN Bridges for Enterprise)

If UDP Hole Punching fails (500 ms timeout) because a corporate banking AI agent sits behind a Symmetric NAT, routing through an intermediary kicks in.

This is where the super-nodes come into play:

Bridge request (Allocate Request): Agent A asks a trusted Super-Node to allocate a Relay port (create a TURN session).

Tunnel formation: The Super-Node opens a TCP/WSS socket and tells both agents its address.

End-to-end proxying: The agents connect to the Super-Node as ordinary clients. The Super-Node blindly forwards encrypted bytes from A to B and back.

Payment for relaying: a delivered H2H message — text of up to 64 KB — costs $0.001, paid to the super-node that delivered it (changelog entries 33 and 52); attachments never travel through a super-node. Whether and how a super-node is paid for other traffic it relays is an open question of the changelog (document 000); until it is decided, that relaying is described without a price. A super-node is paid its share of the period's fee pool and the search and delivery fees (documents 05, 09, 17).

## 2.5 Connection Establishment State Machine

The network stack logic inside the client SDK (Rust / Go) is implemented as follows:

Gathering all candidates (Local IP, Public STUN IP, Relay IP).

Parallel ping (Connectivity Checks) across all routes at once.

Priority selection (Nomination):

Priority 0: Local network (LAN) — 0 ms.

Priority 1: UDP Hole Punching — 10-50 ms (Free).

Priority 2: TCP Relay Fallback — 50-150 ms (relayed by a super-node).

In this way we guarantee 100% packet deliverability (Reachability) in any network topology, from a smart home to the closed perimeters of the Fortune 500, without breaking decentralization.

en.title: 3. Encryption and Proxying: Envoy Proxy, Web3-mTLS and E2EE Isolation
en.text:
# 3. Encryption and Proxying: Envoy Proxy, Web3-mTLS and E2EE Isolation

Separating discovery and connection logic (the Control Plane: announcements, the super-nodes' Kademlia table and the rendezvous of document 02) from data transfer (the Data Plane) is a classic pattern of high-load systems. In the reference implementation the role of the Data Plane is played by an integrated Envoy Proxy instance; any program that gives the encrypted channel of document 19 may take its place. This provides microsecond latencies, L4/L7 load balancing and hardware-accelerated encryption, leaving Super-Nodes with the sole function of "blind routers".

## 3.1 Envoy Proxy as the Data Plane (Sidecar Pattern)

In the reference implementation every AI agent (both client and provider) is deployed together with a lightweight Envoy sidecar container.

Envoy functions: Managing timeouts, retries, circuit breaking when a node goes down, and keeping persistent connections (keep-alive HTTP/2 and gRPC).

Dynamic configuration (xDS API): Envoy does not use static configuration files. The local Lagrix client (Control Plane) keeps the addresses it learns — from announcements (document 17), from the rendezvous and from the relays (document 02). As soon as it learns a new address of the needed Provider or a backup Relay bridge, the client sends this data over gRPC (through the EDS/CDS protocols) directly into Envoy's memory. The proxy rebuilds routes on the fly, without a restart, providing zero downtime (Zero Downtime Routing).

## 3.2 Web3-Native mTLS (Mutual Authentication)

In corporate networks (Zero Trust) the security standard is Mutual TLS (mTLS), where server and client check each other's certificates. In a decentralized Web3 network there are no central Certificate Authorities (such as Verisign). Lagrix solves this with elliptic-curve cryptography (secp256k1).

Ephemeral key generation: When a session starts, Envoy generates a temporary TLS certificate (x509).

Web3 signature: The local agent takes this certificate and signs it with the key of its node's wallet — the one wallet through which the node's elements pay and are paid (changelog entries 22 and 39).

Cryptographic handshake:

Agent A connects to Agent B.

They exchange certificates and Web3 signatures.

Each extracts the public address (Ethereum Address) from the signature and checks that it matches the other side's node wallet recorded in the escrow deal (document 04, section 4.1).

Result: The agents mathematically prove their identity at the transport level. A Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack is impossible: even if an attacker intercepts the IP, they cannot forge the wallet's cryptographic signature.

## 3.3 E2EE and Payload Isolation (Payload Blindness)

This is the most important point for maintaining the legal status of a "Mere Conduit" (Neutral provider). The infrastructure (Super-Nodes/Relays) must physically be unable to read the context of an AI request (Prompt) or the answer (Inference Result).

A multi-layer envelope architecture (Onion-lite routing) is used:

Outer layer (Transport): Envoy encapsulates packets in a standard TLS 1.3 tunnel to the Super-Node. The Super-Node sees only headers: sender IP, recipient IP, packet size — enough to route the packet and nothing more.

Inner layer (Payload E2EE): The data itself (for example, JSON with a system prompt) is encrypted with a symmetric key (AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). This key is generated through the Diffie-Hellman protocol (ECDH) exclusively between the Client and the Provider during the handshake.

Legal shield: A Super-Node passing traffic through itself operates on an encrypted Blob object (a black box). If illegal or toxic content is transferred inside, the Super-Node owner is protected by cryptography: they will mathematically prove in any court that they had no decryption keys, and therefore could not perform moderation (DPI).

## 3.4 Metadata Obfuscation (Protection Against Traffic Analysis)

Even if a Super-Node does not see the content, attackers can analyze packet sizes (Traffic Pattern Analysis). For example, a short request and a long answer is a typical pattern of LLM text generation.
To protect the confidentiality of corporate clients:

Padding: Envoy automatically pads encrypted E2EE packets with random bytes up to fixed sizes (for example, 4KB, 16KB, 64KB).

Effect: To an outside observer (and to the Super-Node) all passing traffic looks like an absolutely uniform stream of binary blocks of the same size. Identifying the nature of the task (video generation, code search or a transactional request) becomes impossible.

## 3.5 Keys of H2H conversations and A2A deals (changelog entry 33)

**H2H — MLS (IETF RFC 9420).** People's conversations are encrypted with the open MLS standard: the key changes with every message, so a
key stolen today does not open yesterday's messages, and after the next key update not future ones either. A node's public key package
is signed by the node's wallet: the other side checks the signature and knows which wallet's owner it talks to. A super-node serves as the
delivery service: it keeps only public key packages, relays and holds encrypted messages — text of up to 64 KB, held for an offline
recipient for up to 30 days and up to 1 MB per recipient; it has no private keys. Conversations are never written to a blockchain.

**Attachments (changelog entry 52).** A file never travels through a super-node. The sender encrypts it with a random key, keeps it on
its own node or in storage it chooses, and puts into the MLS message the file's name, size and type, a download address that cannot be
guessed and expires, the key and the hash of the file. Only the recipient can open the file, and the hash shows that it was not changed
after sending.

**A2A — a one-time session key.** A deal's key is created at the handshake (ECDH, section 3.3) and deleted when the session ends.

en.title: 4. The Escrow Smart Contract: A2AEscrow.sol (EIP-712, Time-Lock, Fee and Receipts)
en.text:
# 4. The Escrow Smart Contract: A2AEscrow.sol (EIP-712, Time-Lock, Fee and Receipts)

The A2AEscrow.sol smart contract is the financial core of Lagrix. Its job is to guarantee, without the parties having to trust each
other, that the Provider gets paid for completed work and the Customer cannot take the result without paying. Writing large data to a
blockchain is expensive, so the contract works only with lightweight cryptographic hashes and signatures; the agents' requests and
results stay in the P2P network.

A closed deal in this contract is the source of everything else in the network: the fee is taken from it (document 09), a receipt is
born from it (document 05), the reviews of both sides are bound to it (document 17), and the participants' history is updated.

## 4.1 The deal life cycle

The escrow logic is a strict finite state machine.

```solidity
enum TaskState { UNINITIALIZED, LOCKED, COMMITTED, COMPLETED, REFUNDED, CANCELLED }

struct Task {
    uint96 amount;        // the network part of the payment, in USDC (up to $79 billion, 96 bits are enough)
    uint40 lockedAt;      // when the funds were locked
    uint40 commitTime;    // when the Provider submitted the result
    uint40 deliverBy;     // the delivery deadline: the last moment the Provider may record delivery (section 4.3)
    uint32 disputeWindow; // the dispute window: seconds after delivery for the Customer to accept or cancel (section 4.3)
    TaskState state;      // current state
    address customer;     // the Customer's node wallet
    address provider;     // the Provider's node wallet — the only one who may perform the task
    address superNode;    // the super-node the deal passed through
    bytes32 customerElement; // the Customer's element that orders the work
    bytes32 element;      // the Provider's element that does the work
    bytes32 agent;        // the agent of that element
    address developer;    // the developer of an element received over F2F, named by the Provider in commitResult (document 26)
}

uint256 constant MAX_DELIVERY = 90 days;       // the delivery deadline is at most 90 days after the lock
uint256 constant MAX_DISPUTE_WINDOW = 14 days; // the dispute window is at most 14 days
```

The fields are packed tightly: a deal record takes a few storage slots, which keeps the cost on layer-2 networks minimal.

- **LOCKED.** The Customer locks USDC in the contract, names the Provider's address and sets the two deadlines of the deal
  (section 4.3). Nobody else can take over the order.
- **COMMITTED.** The Provider has done the work, sent the result over the P2P network and recorded the submission in the contract,
  starting the timer.
- **COMPLETED.** The deal is closed: the Provider receives the payment minus the fee, the fee goes to the period's pool — less the
  developer share when the Provider works with an element received over F2F (section 4.4) —
  and a receipt is recorded (section 4.5).
- **REFUNDED.** The Provider declined the task (`declineTask`) — for any reason, which the network does not judge — or the delivery
  deadline passed with no delivery and the Customer took the money back (`claimRefund`, section 4.3). The funds return to the Customer
  in full, and no fee is taken.
- **CANCELLED.** The Customer did not accept the delivered work and cancelled the order within the dispute window (section 4.3). The
  refund is at most the weight of the Customer's likes as a customer, and the same weight is deducted from its likes; the Provider receives the rest,
  less the fee on it; both sides may review the order, no receipt is written, and a «cancelled order» is recorded for both sides
  (document 17; changelog entries 42, 46 and 55).

## 4.2 Cryptographic receipts (EIP-712)

The contract does not know whether the Provider actually did the work: it sees only signatures. Closing a deal therefore relies on
the EIP-712 standard (Typed Data Hashing and Signing).

- **Off-chain signature.** The Customer receives the result over the P2P channel; its agent checks the data and, if everything is
  correct, signs an acceptance: `{ "taskId": 12345, "resultHash": "0xabc...", "amount": 5000000 }`.
- **On-chain execution.** The Provider submits this signature (v, r, s) to the contract with `executeTask()`.
- **Verification.** The contract recovers the address from the signature (`ecrecover`). If it is the Customer of this deal, the deal
  moves to COMPLETED.

The network itself never judges whether a service was delivered. Acceptance belongs to the Customer; quality is told by the reviews of
both sides (document 17) and by the pages their authors may attach to them (document 25).

## 4.3 Time-Lock: the delivery deadline and the dispute window

A Customer could receive the result, go offline and never send the signature, freezing the Provider's payment; a Provider could take
an order and never deliver, freezing the Customer's. Every deal therefore carries two deadlines of its own, set by the Customer when it
locks the payment and seen by the Provider before it starts work (changelog, entry 53). How they are chosen for instant and deferred
deals and for a series of deals is described in document 27.

- **Lock.** `lockFunds(…, deliverBy, disputeWindow)` writes both deadlines into the deal. The contract rejects a delivery deadline that
  is not in the future or lies more than `MAX_DELIVERY` (90 days) after the lock, and a dispute window longer than `MAX_DISPUTE_WINDOW`
  (14 days).
- **Decline.** Until it records delivery, the Provider may call `declineTask(taskId)`: the whole amount returns to the Customer, the deal
  moves to REFUNDED and no fee is taken.
- **Commitment.** Having finished the work, the Provider calls `commitResult(taskId, resultHash, developer)`: the deal moves to COMMITTED
  and the contract records the time. `developer` names the developer of the element the Provider works with, when it received that element
  over F2F, and is empty for its own element (document 26). The contract accepts delivery only while `block.timestamp <= deliverBy`: a
  delivery recorded later is rejected.
- **Refund after the deadline.** If the delivery deadline has passed with no delivery, the Customer calls `claimRefund(taskId)`: the
  whole amount returns to the Customer, the deal moves to REFUNDED, no fee is taken and no receipt is written.
- **Dispute window.** After delivery the Customer has the dispute window of this deal (`disputeWindow`) to send the signature.
- **Cancellation.** Within the same window the Customer may refuse the result and call `cancelOrder(taskId)` instead of signing. The
  contract reads the Customer's like weight as a customer (document 17), returns `min(likeWeight, amount)` to the Customer, deducts
  the same weight from its likes as a new event with its date and sends the rest to the Provider; the deal moves to CANCELLED. A Customer with no likes gets
  nothing back: the whole amount goes to the Provider. The fee is taken from the part the Provider receives and divided as on
  COMPLETED (section 4.4); both sides may review the order, each review weighing that fee; no receipt is written (changelog, entry 55).
  A refund of the whole amount takes no fee and gives no review.
- **Automatic closing.** When the window has passed, the Provider calls `claimTimeout(taskId)`. The contract checks
  `block.timestamp > commitTime + disputeWindow` and closes the deal without the Customer's signature — with the same fee and the same
  receipt as a normal closing.

## 4.4 Splitting the payment and the fee

When a deal moves to COMPLETED, the contract splits the network part; when an order is CANCELLED, it splits the same way the part left to
the Provider after the refund (section 4.3):

| To whom | Share | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The Provider | the rest (95% while the fee is 5%) | to the wallet of the Provider's node |
| The network fee | at most 5%, set by modelling | into the pool of the current period, divided among super-nodes under document 09 |
| The developer share | 20% of the fee, only when the Provider works with an element it received over F2F | to the `developer` wallet of the element's F2F card (document 26) |

The pool of each period is divided in equal parts among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in that period; the parties of
the deal never receive it (document 09). The developer of an element received over F2F is not a party: the Provider's node names it
in `commitResult` (section 4.3), and its share leaves the fee when the deal moves to COMPLETED or CANCELLED (document 26). The fee is taken from the very
first deal (document 05, section 5.3).

## 4.5 The receipt and the participants' history

A closed deal (COMPLETED) emits an event from which receipts and history are built; a cancelled order emits none (changelog, entry 55):

```solidity
event Receipt(
    uint256 indexed taskId,
    address indexed superNode,
    address customer,
    address provider,
    bytes32 customerElement,
    bytes32 element,
    bytes32 agent,
    address developer,
    uint96 amount
);
```

- **The receipt.** A `Receipt` event records the network part of the deal, the element and agent that did the work, the element that
  ordered it and the developer named for the deal, if any; the reviews of both sides are bound to these elements (document 17). It counts for
  the customer, the provider and the super-node `superNode`, each with a weight equal to that amount. Receipts order search results by
  the last twelve months of paid work (document 17) and measure the paid work that opens a super-node place (document 05, section 5.6). Which
  super-node a deal names in `superNode` is set by the customer when funds are locked; how this field is tied to the node that actually
  served the deal is an open question of the changelog (document 000).
- **The participants' history.** The contract updates, for both parties, the number of closed deals and the time of the last deal —
  separately as provider and as customer. The number of deals is history, not reputation (document 17).

## 4.6 The network part of a deal

A deal may be paid in two parts. The parties may pay any part outside the network, in any ordinary way, and lock the rest in escrow.

- **The network sees only its part.** Only the amount locked in escrow is recorded, takes the fee and leaves a receipt. The part paid
  outside the network leaves no trace in Lagrix.
- **Only the network part counts.** The weight of the receipt, the weight of both sides' reviews, and the place in search all follow
  the network part.
- **Protection differs.** The network part is protected by escrow until acceptance. The part paid outside the network is protected by
  the law of the country where the deal was made, not by Lagrix.

The more of a deal the parties put through the network, the more it counts for their reputation. People may start with ordinary
payments and move more of each deal into the network as their reputation grows.

## 4.7 Cost

Tight field packing and EIP-712 signatures instead of stored strings keep the contract cheap on layer-2 networks (Arbitrum, Base) —
hundredths of a cent per operation. This is critical for micro-deals between AI agents.

en.title: 5. Fees and Reputation
en.text:
# 5. Fees and Reputation

The Lagrix network's money is USDC: the part of a deal paid through the network is deposited in escrow, the network takes a fee on it,
and search and message delivery are paid from a prepaid deposit, one voucher per super-node carrying a running total (changelog entry 52). This document describes what the network charges, where the fees go,
what answers for a super-node's honesty, and how super-nodes join.

All rules here live in immutable contracts: no administrator key, no upgrade key, no parameter anyone can change after deployment.
New rules can arrive only as a new version of the contracts that participants join voluntarily (document 18). The numbers that are
not fixed below are set once, by modelling, before deployment.

## 5.1 Key properties

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| The network's money | USDC (document 04) |
| Deal fee | a constant of at most 5% of the network part of a deal, set by modelling (5% until then), divided equally among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in the period (section 5.3, document 09); 20% of it — 1% of the deal at a 5% fee — goes to the developer of an element the provider received over F2F, so the pool receives 4% of such a deal and 5% of a deal made with the provider's own element (document 26) |
| Search and delivery | $0.01 per result list and $0.001 per text message of up to 64 KB a super-node delivers, from a prepaid USDC balance in the contract: one voucher per super-node carries the running total and is redeemed once per period, and a withdrawal waits (document 17, section 17.8; changelog entry 52) |
| First-contact rate | set by an agent for a first request to it and paid to its wallet, once, when it reads the request; not returned on a no (document 23) |
| Official mark | $100 per application, not returned; divided equally among the members of the panel who voted (document 24) |
| Gas | everyone pays for their own actions: in the network's ether or through a third-party gas payment service (document 08) |
| What answers for honesty | a super-node's place and reputation (section 5.4) |
| Weight of a review | the fee paid on the deal (document 17, section 17.5) |
| Review page | the address of a page attached to a review by its author; no fee and no weight — the author pays only gas (document 25) |
| Founder's share | none: the founder takes part on the same terms as anyone (section 5.5) |

## 5.2 Receipts

Bitcoin pays miners for computations that are useless in themselves, because Bitcoin is its own ledger: proof of work decides who
writes the next block and makes rewriting history expensive. Lagrix keeps its escrow and its records in contracts on an EVM layer-2
network (Arbitrum, Base), which already orders transactions and protects history. Lagrix therefore needs no mining: it records what the
network exists for — paid deals between agents.

**Receipt.** When a deal between a customer and a provider is closed in escrow (document 04), the contract records a receipt — a record
of a completed, paid deal for the customer, the provider and the super-node it passed through, naming the element and the agent that did
the work. A receipt's weight is the network part of the deal in USDC, not the number of messages: a thousand messages inside one deal
give one receipt, and a part paid outside the network gives none (document 04, section 4.6).

Receipts are what the rest of the network stands on: search ranking follows the receipts of the last twelve months (document 17), a
super-node place goes to owners of provider agents by the receipts of their paid work (section 5.6), and every review belongs to the deal
of one receipt (document 17, section 17.5). A receipt cannot be forged: it is the closing of a paid deal.

## 5.3 The deal fee

The network takes a fee on the network part of every deal, in USDC. Its size is a constant in code, set by modelling and never above 5%;
until the modelling is done, it is 5%. The fees of a period are pooled and divided in equal parts among the super-nodes that passed the
quality minimum in that period; the parties of a deal never receive it. When the provider works with an element it received over F2F, 20%
of the fee goes to the developer of that element and the rest to the pool (document 26). At a 5% fee this is one rule in two cases:
with an element received over F2F, 1% of the deal goes to its developer and 4% into the pool; with the provider's own element, all 5%
go into the pool. The fee is taken from the very first deal; nothing is kept back
for later periods. The full rules are in document 09.

The fee pays super-nodes for the work they do all the time — search, connections and the index of receipts and reviews — and it is how
fake deals are made to cost real money. A review weighs exactly the fee paid on its deal (document 17, section 17.5), so a deal with
oneself, made to collect reviews, buys one unit of review weight for one dollar of fees: weight can never be had for less than it weighs.
The one exception is stated in document 26: in a deal with itself, a node that names a wallet of its own as the developer gets the 20%
developer share back, so its weight costs it 80 cents on the dollar.

## 5.4 Reputation answers for honesty

What a super-node has at stake is its place and its reputation:

- **A proven violation leaves a mark.** When a violation is proven (document 06, section 6.3), a permanent, visible «proven violation»
  mark is added to the node's wallet and to all its elements. The mark is a new event in the record: nothing is erased or rewritten
  (document 17).
- **The place is lost for good.** The node leaves its place at once and may not hold a super-node place again. Its elements keep working
  as customers and providers, and every counterparty sees the mark.
- **A new element starts from zero.** Its way to a place is the same as anyone's — paid work near the median (section 5.6).
