- **Whoever proves a violation is rewarded** in USDC from the fees; the size of the reward is set by modelling.

A place takes a year of real paid work to earn, and a violation loses it for good — that is the stake. Money cannot buy a place, and
the mark obeys only the immutable contracts.

## 5.5 No founder share

The founder receives no share of anything: no share of the fees, no tranche, no pre-allocation. No key changes a rule.

The founder and persons related to them, Fractera, Inc. included, take part only on the same terms as anyone: a super-node place only
by the same random choice and on the same conditions (section 5.6), provider agents paid by the same rules. There is no privilege and no
exclusion.

At the launch of the network the founder also takes on public commitments of their own: one publicly named node, no deals between the
founder's own elements, and, until ten super-nodes pass the quality minimum in a period, no share of the fees — it stays in the pool of
the other super-nodes (document 000, entries 41 and 42); and no developer share from the founder's named node (entry 51). They are
commitments of a person, not rules of the contracts.

## 5.6 How new super-nodes join

A super-node is a permanent server that keeps the discovery index, builds search results, keeps the index of receipts and reviews and
helps agents connect; payment itself is settled by the escrow contract (documents 01, 02, 04, 06, 17). A super-node place is not bought
and not taken by number: places have no stages and no numbers, and the terms are the same on any day (document 000, entries 31 and 40).

- **Only owners of provider agents.** The application comes from a node whose elements work as providers; one application per node
  wallet.
- **The measure is paid work.** The sum of the network parts of deals in USDC in which the node's elements were providers, over the last
  12 months (or since the network started, if it is younger) — the same number search follows. Karma is not part of it: it lives outside
  the network.
- **A window around the median.** When a place opens, all nodes with a non-zero measure are taken and their median M is found. Nodes with
  a measure from 0.75 × M to 1.25 × M can apply. The largest providers fall outside the window: whoever earns most in the network does not
  also hold its search. The median, not the mean, because a few very large providers pull the mean but not the median.
- **Random choice with diversity.** When a place opens, the contract puts the applicants in the window in a random order, keeping
  diversity of networks and regions, so that one applicant with many servers cannot take many places. It computes the randomness itself
  with commit and reveal: when applying, an applicant publishes the hash of its secret; after applications close, it reveals the secret;
  all revealed secrets together decide the order. Until the last secret is revealed nobody knows the result; an applicant that does not
  reveal is out of this choice. No oracle and no outside service are needed. Ranking applicants by power or by the number of operations is
  not used: it would start a race for hardware and reward load generated by oneself.
- **An invitation and 48 hours.** The first applicant in the order receives an invitation. Within 48 hours it deploys its server, catches up
  the announcements of the kinds it will hold from their other holders (document 17, section 17.12) and submits it for the check by agents of the network's nodes taken in turn — not by super-nodes: existing super-nodes gain from having
  fewer competitors, so they must not be the ones who judge newcomers. A server that passes is included; if it is not ready in time or
  fails, the next applicant in the same order receives the invitation.
- **A clean record.** A node with a «proven violation» mark cannot apply (section 5.4).
- **How many places.** There are always at least ten places. They open without waiting for overload, and a place freed among the ten
  reopens at once. Beyond ten, new places open only when the network is overloaded — when deals, redeemed searches or delivered messages per super-node exceed their constants (changelog entry 47) — two at
  a time.
- **Overload.** Once both new super-nodes are included, one super-node leaves: the one with the worst results in the period's checks
  under load — response time and refusals. There is no penalty. Each overload adds one super-node, and the network replaces its weakest
  link by the service it gave under load, not by declared hardware.
- **The start.** While no node has paid work, the window is empty and anyone can apply; the same invitation and the same 48 hours apply.
  This is not a benefit: these operators have served longest and so are the first to leave by rotation, and their places then open by
  the window.
- **Rotation.** Once every 1 year / N, where N is the number of super-nodes, the super-node that has served longest leaves — but only
  after its successor has passed the check and been included; until then it keeps working. There is no penalty. Each super-node stays
  about a year, so the door stays open to those who do paid work now, and capacity does not dip while a place changes hands.
- **The quality minimum.** Every period, agents taken in turn check each super-node against a minimum, its index included (document 17, section 17.12): passed or failed. Those who passed
  share the period's fee pool equally (section 5.3, document 09); a super-node that fails for several periods leaves.
- **Requirements grow.** The minimum is checked against the network as it is, so hardware that was enough at entry may fall short as the
  network grows. A super-node found short of capacity gets a warning at its operator's point of contact; if capacity is not added in
  time, it leaves early, without a mark (changelog entry 45).
- **Vacancies.** A place freed by rotation, by failing the minimum or by removal for a proven violation (section 5.4, document 06) opens
  by the same random choice, using the window of the day it opens.
- **The cost we do not hide.** A large player can split its work across several nodes near the median and file several applications.
  Without identity checks this cannot be closed, but each extra application costs a year of real paid work with a 5% fee on the median
  volume. Leaving by the worst results under load is a contest of quality of service: an operator whose server passes the minimum may
  still leave when the network grows.

The numbers — the overload constant, how many failed periods lead to leaving, the reward to whoever proves a violation — are set by
modelling. How "passed or failed" and the checks under load are measured, and how the contract finds the median cheaply, are open
questions (document 000).

## 5.7 What a super-node is paid for

This is the whole list, in one place; other documents refer here. Everything is paid in USDC, for work, under rules fixed in the
contracts. How much a super-node earns is not known in advance and not guaranteed: it depends on the deals of the network and on how many
super-nodes pass the quality minimum.

| What | How much | Where the rule is |
|---|---|---|
| An equal share of the period's fee pool | the pool receives 4% of every deal made with an element received over F2F (1% goes to the element's developer) and 5% of every deal made with the provider's own element, at a 5% fee; it is divided equally among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in the period | section 5.3, documents 09, 26 |
| Redistribution of shares | a super-node that fails the quality minimum in a period — downtime, failed checks — receives no share of that period's pool, and the pool is divided only among those that passed; the founder's share stays in the pool of the others in the same way until ten super-nodes pass the minimum (section 5.5) | section 5.6, documents 06, 09 |
| Search | $0.01 for every result list it builds | document 17, section 17.8 |
| Message delivery | $0.001 for every H2H message it delivers; text up to 64 KB | documents 17, 21; changelog entries 33 and 52 |
| A vote on the Official mark | an equal share of the $100 fee of an application, among the panel members who voted — about $11 for nine votes | document 24 |
| Proving a violation by another super-node | a reward from the fees, its size set by modelling | document 06, section 6.4 |

What a super-node loses goes to the others: downtime and a failed minimum cost it its share of the period's pool, which the super-nodes
that passed divide among themselves (document 06, section 6.2); a proven violation also costs it the place, with a permanent mark
(section 5.4). What a super-node does not earn is part of the list too: the parties of a deal
never receive the fee, and a super-node takes nothing from the deals it serves beyond the fees above.

en.title: 6. Super-nodes: Downtime and Proven Violations
en.text:
# 6. Super-nodes: Downtime and Proven Violations

Super-nodes are the backbone of Lagrix: they keep the discovery table, build search results, keep the index of receipts and reviews and
help agents connect; payment itself is settled by the escrow contract (document 04). The SuperNodeRegistry.sol contract keeps the
super-node places and the record of proven violations. What a super-node has at stake is its place and its reputation (document 05,
section 5.4). The main rule of this document: **downtime is not a violation**. A server that goes offline simply stops
earning; a mark is added only for a proven violation.

## 6.1 What the contract keeps

```solidity
struct SuperNode {
    uint40 includedAt;      // when the place was taken (rotation order)
    uint40 lastSeen;        // last confirmed availability
    bool   active;          // holds a place now
    address pubKeyAddress;  // address bound to the NodeID
    string  relay;          // address of its Nostr relay (document 17, section 17.12)
}
mapping(address => bool) public provenViolation;  // node wallet => permanent mark; such a node may not hold a place again
```

The mark belongs to the node's wallet and is shown on every element of that node (document 17). It is never removed.

## 6.2 Downtime is not a violation

As in Bitcoin, where a miner that is switched off simply finds no blocks, a super-node is not penalised for downtime.

- **While the node is unavailable,** it serves nobody, so it does not pass the period's quality minimum and receives no share of the
  period's fee pool and no search or delivery fees. It loses only income.
- **Availability** is measured by the same checks that decide the quality minimum — agents of the network's nodes taken in turn
  (changelog entry 30), not competing super-nodes (document 05, section 5.6). The PING of the Kademlia table only keeps routing tables
  fresh (document 01).
- **If the node is unavailable for 30 days in a row, or fails the quality minimum for several periods,** it is removed. Its place
  reopens on the terms of the day it reopens (document 05, section 5.6). It receives no mark: it did not cheat — it left.
- **Leaving early after an unanswered capacity warning** is not a penalty either: there is no mark (changelog entry 45).
- **An index that misses announcements** of the kinds the super-node holds (document 17, section 17.12) is treated like downtime: the
  super-node fails the check and loses income, without a mark.
- **Leaving by rotation or by overload is not a penalty either;** the rules are in document 05, section 5.6.

## 6.3 Violations and their proof

A blockchain cannot see IP packets, so a violation is proven by receipts and checks that anyone can repeat.

**Packet dropping.** A customer (agent A) sends traffic to a provider (agent B) through super-node R. Agent A signs the packet;
agent B signs a receipt of delivery. If R accepted the packet for relaying but B's receipt is missing, agent A sends a
`TRACE_REQUEST`; three independent neighbours confirm that R accepted the packet and did not pass it on — this forms a proof.

**Falsified results.** The place given in turn in search results is calculated verifiably (document 17, section 17.3). A result list in
which that place does not match the calculation is a ready proof: the contract checks the super-node's signature on it and the
calculation data.

**Forged tables and NodeID hijacking.** An attempt to forge Kademlia DHT records or to impersonate another node is proven by
signatures that do not match the node's key.

## 6.4 What a proven violation costs

| Violation | Proof | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Downtime | unavailability in the checks by agents | **none**; the node loses income and after 30 days is removed without a mark |
| Packet dropping | a proof with a missing receipt | the «proven violation» mark, removal, no place ever again |
| Falsified results | results that do not match the verifiable calculation | the same |
| Forged tables, NodeID hijacking | signatures that do not match | the same |

A proven violation adds a permanent, visible «proven violation» mark to the node's wallet and to all its elements; the node leaves its
place at once and may not hold a super-node place again. Nothing is erased: the mark is a new event in the record, and the node's earlier
history stays as it was (document 05, section 5.4). Whoever proved the violation receives a reward in USDC from the fees; its size is set
by modelling.

```
[Customer agent] --(packet)--> [Super-node R] --X (dropped)--> [Provider agent]
       |                                                              |
       +---------------- (TRACE_REQUEST, waiting for receipt) --------+
                                      |
                                   [Proof]
                                      |
                                      v
                   [SuperNodeRegistry.sol: proveViolation()]
                                      |
                    +-----------------+-----------------+
                    |                                   |
     (mark on the wallet and its elements,    (reward in USDC from the fees
      removal, no place again)                  to whoever proved it)
```

## 6.5 Protection against false reports

So that the contract is not flooded with fake proofs, calling `proveViolation()` requires the reporter to lock a small amount of USDC.

- **The proof is valid:** the reporter gets the amount back and receives the reward.
- **The proof is false:** the amount is lost for good — sent to an address whose key nobody has, so that nobody gains from a false report.

Honest work pays better than a false report, and a false report costs more than silence.

en.title: 7. Smart Contract Testing and Audit: Foundry, Slither and Fuzzing
en.text:
# 7. Smart Contract Testing and Audit: Foundry, Slither and Fuzzing

Lagrix smart contracts handle real money (USDC). A bug in a contract is dangerous: the contracts are immutable, with no
administrator or upgrade key (document 18), so a deployed contract cannot be fixed at all — a bug is closed only by a new version that
participants move to. Every contract therefore passes three layers of checks before deployment: Foundry tests, invariant fuzzing and
Slither static analysis.

| Contract | What it does | Document |
|---|---|---|
| A2AEscrow.sol | deals, receipts, Time-Lock with the delivery deadline and dispute window of each deal, cancellation, fee deduction, the `Receipt` event | 04, 27 |
| FeeDistributor.sol | the fee pool of each period and its equal division among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum | 09 |
| SearchVouchers.sol | prepaid balances with a withdrawal delay; one voucher per payee carrying a running total for searches, delivered messages and first-contact rates, redeemed once per period | 17, 23 |
| SuperNodeRegistry.sol | places, removal, «proven violation» marks, false reports | 05, 06 |
| FeedbackRegistry.sol | reviews of both sides bound to completed deals and to cancelled orders with a fee, weighted by the fee paid on the deal, per element and role; every indicator a count and a sum, unreviewed deals, negative ratings (dislikes given against the reviewable weight), likes deducted by cancellations; the address of a review page, attached once by the review's author | 17, 25 |
| OfficialMarks.sol | the Official marks: applications with the $100 fee, panels of nine chosen at random with commit and reveal, votes, challenges and the founder's mark written at deployment | 24 |

## 7.1 Unit and integration tests (Foundry)

Foundry tests are written in Solidity itself and run at the speed of compiled code. Key scenarios:

- `test_A2AEscrow_StateTransitions()` — LOCKED → COMMITTED → COMPLETED transitions and rejection of invalid calls (for example,
  `claimTimeout()` before the dispute window expires).
- `test_Deadlines_Limits()` — a lock whose delivery deadline is not in the future or lies more than 90 days ahead, or whose dispute
  window is longer than 14 days, is rejected.
- `test_Deadline_LateDeliveryRejected()` — `commitResult()` after `deliverBy` is rejected.
- `test_ClaimRefund_AfterDeadline()` — `claimRefund()` returns the whole amount and moves the deal to REFUNDED only after `deliverBy`
  and only with no delivery; it takes no fee and writes no receipt; before the deadline or after a delivery it is rejected.
- `test_DeclineTask()` — the provider declines before delivery and the whole amount returns with no fee; after delivery a decline is
  rejected.
- `test_DisputeWindow_PerDeal()` — two deals with different dispute windows close each on its own timer.
- `test_EIP712_SignatureReplay()` — a signature cannot be reused with another `taskId` or nonce.
- `test_FeeSplit_95_5()` — on closing, the fee is exactly the constant rate of the network part (5% until modelling sets it, never above 5%) and the provider gets the rest; a refund takes no fee.
- `test_DeveloperShare()` — with a `developer` named for a deal on an element received over F2F, 20% of the fee goes to that wallet and 80% to the pool of the period; with no `developer`, the whole fee goes to the pool; a refund pays neither.
- `test_FeePool_EqualShares()` — the fees of a period go into its pool and are divided equally among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum; the parties of a deal and super-nodes that failed the minimum receive nothing; nothing carries over to the next period.
- `test_Voucher_RunningTotal()` — a voucher pays only the difference between its total and the total already redeemed for that payer and payee; a voucher whose total did not grow pays nothing; a voucher not signed by the payer is rejected; a withdrawal waits the delay, and a voucher signed before it is still paid.
- `test_Review_Weight()` — a review needs a completed deal or a cancelled order with a fee, one per side, and weighs the fee paid on it; a second review of the same deal by the same side is rejected.
- `test_Reputation_CountAndSum()` — every indicator updates its count and its sum together; a review, a like or a dislike, removes the deal from «unreviewed».
- `test_Reputation_AllOrders()` — every paid order adds to «all orders» of both sides, completed or cancelled; a proven-violation mark on the node's wallet shows on every element of the node.
- `test_Reputation_NegativeRatings()` — a dislike adds its weight to the reviewer's «dislikes given»; every completed deal and every cancelled order with a fee adds its fee to the reviewable weight of both sides; negative ratings, read as dislikes given ÷ reviewable weight, stay between 0% and 100%.
- `test_ReviewPage_Once()` — only the side that gave a review attaches a page to it, once; a second page on the same review and a page on a deal the sender has not reviewed are rejected; the like or dislike, its weight and every indicator stay unchanged; an address longer than the limit is rejected.
- `test_Cancel_RefundByLikes()` — a cancellation within the dispute window refunds `min(likeWeight, amount)`, deducts the same weight from the customer's likes as a new event, sends the rest to the provider less the fee on it, records a cancelled order for both and writes no receipt; a customer without likes gets nothing back; a refund of the whole amount takes no fee and opens no review.
- `test_NoAdminFunctions()` — no function changes a rate, a price or a threshold after deployment.
- `test_Downtime_NoMark()` — an unavailable node is not penalised and after 30 days is removed without a mark.
- `test_ProvenViolation_MarkAndReward()` — a valid proof adds a permanent mark to the node's wallet, removes it from its place, blocks any new place and pays the reporter's reward in USDC; a false proof loses the reporter's locked amount.

```solidity
// Example: Time-Lock in A2AEscrow.t.sol — the dispute window belongs to the deal (changelog, entry 53)
function test_CannotClaimTimeoutBeforeDisputeWindow() public {
    vm.prank(customer);
    // lock 100 USDC (6 decimals) for a deferred deal: deliver within a day, a dispute window of 24 hours
    escrow.lockFunds(taskId, provider, superNode, 100 * 10**6, uint40(block.timestamp + 1 days), 24 hours);

    vm.prank(provider);
    escrow.commitResult(taskId, resultHash, address(0)); // no developer: the provider's own element (document 26)

    // try to collect 2 hours after delivery, before the deal's 24-hour window expires
    vm.warp(block.timestamp + 2 hours);

    vm.prank(provider);
    vm.expectRevert(A2AEscrow.DisputeWindowNotExpired.selector);
    escrow.claimTimeout(taskId);
}
```

## 7.2 Fuzzing and invariants

Unit tests check the scenarios the developer thought of. Fuzzing feeds millions of random inputs — edge values, zero addresses, huge
amounts — and checks invariants that must hold for any sequence of calls:

1. **Escrow solvency.** The escrow contract's USDC balance is never below the sum of all locked deals.
2. **Fee solvency.** FeeDistributor's USDC balance is never below the unclaimed part of the period pools.
3. **No founder share.** No address receives fees except super-nodes that passed the quality minimum, the developers named on deals
   (document 26) and the rewards for proven violations.
4. **Marks are permanent.** Once set, a «proven violation» mark is never cleared, and a marked wallet never holds a place.
5. **Likes never go below zero.** A refund never exceeds the weight of likes that remains.
6. **Negative ratings stay in bounds.** The weight of dislikes an element has given in a role never exceeds the reviewable weight of its
   orders in that role.
7. **Every deal can end.** A deal past its delivery deadline with no delivery can always be refunded by the customer, and a delivered
   deal past its dispute window can always be closed by the provider: within 104 days of the lock, every deal has a call that ends it.

```solidity
function invariant_EscrowSolvency() public view {
    assertGe(usdc.balanceOf(address(escrow)), escrow.totalLockedFunds(), "Escrow is insolvent");
}

function invariant_MarkedNeverActive() public view {
    for (uint256 i; i < handler.markedCount(); i++) {
        address wallet = handler.marked(i);
        assertTrue(registry.provenViolation(wallet), "Mark was cleared");
        assertFalse(registry.isActiveSuperNode(wallet), "Marked wallet holds a place");
    }
}
```

## 7.3 Static analysis (Slither)

Slither translates the code into an intermediate representation and looks for common vulnerabilities:

- **Reentrancy:** protection — the checks → effects → interactions order and OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuard`.
- **Authorization via `tx.origin`:** forbidden; Slither warns about any use of it.
- **Unchecked low-level calls:** USDC transfers only through `SafeERC20`.
- **Overflows:** built-in checks of Solidity 0.8+ and strict types (`uint96`, `uint40`) for packed fields.

## 7.4 The check pipeline

Every change to the main branch of the open repository goes through the same chain:

```
[ push / pull request ]
       │
       ├──> 1. forge fmt --check               (formatting)
       ├──> 2. slither . --fail-on high|medium  (static analysis)
       ├──> 3. forge test --gas-report          (tests and gas usage)
       └──> 4. forge test --fuzz-runs 10000     (invariant fuzzing)
```

If even one of 10,000 random calls breaks an invariant, the change is not accepted.

en.title: 8. Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): The UserOperation Structure and Bundler Infrastructure
en.text:
# 8. Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): The UserOperation Structure and Bundler Infrastructure

Autonomous AI agents should not manage native blockchain wallets (EOA), having to calculate gas by hand, watch their ETH/MATIC balance and sign raw base transactions. Lagrix implements an Account Abstraction stack based on the ERC-4337 standard, which turns the node's wallet — the one wallet through which all the node's elements and agents pay (changelog entries 22 and 39) — into a programmable smart account (Smart Contract Wallet).

This fully isolates the agent's application logic from blockchain mechanics: the agent operates on a "request-payment" abstraction in USDC, and all the work with network fees is taken over by special aggregator nodes (Bundlers) and the Paymaster contract.

## 8.1 Anatomy of the UserOperation Structure

Instead of standard Ethereum transactions, AI agents form pseudo-transactions — UserOperation (UserOp) objects. The structure packs the agent's intent and is passed over the P2P network of Bundler nodes outside the blockchain's main mempool.

```solidity
struct UserOperation {
    address sender;             // Address of the node's smart account
    uint256 nonce;              // Unique sequential number (Anti-Replay)
    bytes initCode;             // Smart account creation code (if launched for the first time)
    bytes callData;             // Encoded function call (for example, lockFunds in A2AEscrow)
    uint256 callGasLimit;       // Gas limit for executing the application logic
    uint256 verificationGasLimit; // Gas limit for checking signatures and the Paymaster
    uint256 preVerificationGas; // Gas limit to compensate the Bundler's overhead
    uint256 maxFeePerGas;       // Maximum gas price (EIP-1559)
    uint256 maxPriorityFeePerGas;// Tip to the blockchain miner/validator
    bytes paymasterAndData;     // Paymaster contract address + sponsorship signature/conditions
    bytes signature;            // The AI agent's cryptographic signature (secp256k1 / BLS / Passkey)
}
```

Key fields for payments between agents:

initCode (Lazy Account Deployment): A node's smart account is created without transactions on the blockchain: it is generated off-chain deterministically through CREATE2. The first transaction automatically deploys the account contract thanks to the initCode field.

paymasterAndData: The main integration flag. Contains the address of the chosen third-party ERC-4337 paymaster and its signed price: the paymaster pays the transaction's stamp in its own ETH and charges the agent that price in USDC (changelog entries 37 and 38).

## 8.2 Bundler Infrastructure: Assembling and Packing Meta-Transactions

A Bundler is a specialized infrastructure node (a third-party one: Lagrix network participants do not carry others' transactions for a fee or sell stamps — changelog entry 38) that listens to a separate Alt-Mempool for UserOperations.

```
[Client Agent] ---> (UserOp in USDC) ---> [Alt-Mempool (P2P)]
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                        [ Bundler Node ]
                                                 │
                             (Packing into a bundle: [UserOp1, UserOp2, ...])
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                   [ EntryPoint.sol (On-Chain) ]
                                                 │
                                    ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                                    ▼                         ▼
                          [Paymaster]                 [A2AEscrow.sol]
                         (USDC charged for gas)     (Escrow capture)
```

Step-by-step Bundler algorithm:

Reception and filtering (Validation Phase): The Bundler receives a UserOp through the JSON-RPC method eth_sendUserOperation. It performs an off-chain simulation through the EntryPoint.sol contract, checking:
- The validity of the UserOp.signature.
- The paymaster's signature on the price, the agent's sufficient USDC balance or approval, and the paymaster's sufficient ETH deposit in the EntryPoint.
- The absence of forbidden opcodes (for example, TIMESTAMP, GASPRICE) that could break execution determinism.

Aggregation (Batching): The Bundler combines 10 to 100 valid UserOps from different AI agents into one standard Ethereum transaction.

Submission to the On-Chain EntryPoint: The Bundler calls the function handleOps(UserOperation[] ops, address beneficiary) on the singleton EntryPoint.sol contract.

Gas compensation: The Bundler pays the native L2 network gas (ETH) from its own wallet, and the EntryPoint reimburses it in ETH from the paymaster's deposit; the paymaster in turn charges the agent USDC — no more than the signed price.

## 8.3 The EntryPoint.sol Contract: The Execution Core

The ERC-4337 standard uses a single EntryPoint contract, proven over the years and deployed at the same addresses in all EVM networks. It acts as a trusted orchestrator.

Lifecycle of a handleOps() call inside EntryPoint:

Verification Loop:
- For each UserOp, the sender account is checked.
- If the account has not been created yet, initCode is executed.
- The validateUserOp() function on the node's smart account is called to check the ECDSA signature.
- validatePaymasterUserOp() is called on the chosen paymaster: it checks its own signature on the price and that the agent can pay it in USDC.

Execution Loop:
- EntryPoint executes the callData of each UserOp (for example, sending a call to A2AEscrow.sol).
- The exact amount of gas actually spent is measured.
- The EntryPoint charges gas from the paymaster's ETH deposit and calls its postOp, in which the paymaster charges the agent USDC — no more than the signed price.

## 8.4 Benefits for the Lagrix Ecosystem

Zero friction (Zero Gas Friction): A node only needs to put $10$ USDC on its smart account. Its agents will never need to hold native ETH for transactions.

Session Keys: The node's smart account makes it possible to limit permissions. Each agent can be given a temporary key allowed to spend no more than $1$ USDC per hour and to call exclusively the A2AEscrow.sol contract. If an agent is hacked, the hacker cannot withdraw all the funds from the account.

Atomic Multi-Operations: An agent can do approve(USDC) and lockFunds() in one UserOp, reducing the number of on-chain steps and saving 40% on gas.

## 8.5 Who pays gas (changelog entries 37 and 38)

Under ERC-4337 a paymaster's deposit in the EntryPoint is the network's ether («an amount of Ether (or any L2 native currency)»). The
network has no paymaster of its own, and Lagrix contracts require no particular one.

- **Everyone pays the stamps for their own actions themselves** — in the network's ether or through a third-party gas payment service in
  USDC, for example Circle Paymaster: an open contract, USDC only, no sign-up; on Arbitrum and Base a 10% surcharge on gas. The network
  has no connection with such a service.
- **Network participants do not sell stamps.** Neither nodes nor super-nodes run paymasters for others or carry others' transactions for
  a fee: such a service could count as an exchange of crypto-assets or their transfer on behalf of clients in the sense of MiCA (Article
  3(1)(16), (20), (26)).
- **A super-node pays stamps only for its own actions:** redeeming batches of vouchers, collecting its share of the fees, registering its place.
- **The fallback — one's own ether — is always open:** a third-party service's refusal does not cut a participant off from the network.

Micropayments — search, message delivery and first-contact rates — never go on-chain one by one: a node signs one voucher per payee that
carries the running total, and the payee redeems the latest one once per period (document 17, section 17.8; changelog entry 52), so the
stamp per operation is close to zero.

**Stamp price measured — 14 October 2026, 23:54 UTC.** A simple USDC transfer: Arbitrum One — median **$0.0028** (21 transfers, from
$0.0020 to $0.0032, gas 0.020 gwei); Base — median **$0.00065** (15 transfers, from $0.00055 to $0.0020, gas 0.006 gwei); ETH at $2,416.
Sources: the official public nodes [arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc](https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc) and [mainnet.base.org](https://mainnet.base.org),
the price from [Coinbase](https://api.coinbase.com/v2/prices/ETH-USD/spot). This is a one-minute snapshot: the price changes with network load
and the ether rate. Locking into escrow and accepting work are heavier than a simple transfer — a measurement of the deployed contracts
will show their price. Conclusion: a stamp is a fraction of a cent; a $0.001 message redeemed on its own would lose most of its price to the stamp, so a voucher
carries a running total and is redeemed once per period (changelog entry 52).

en.title: 9. The Deal Fee: Payment to Super-nodes for the Network's Work
en.text:
# 9. The Deal Fee: Payment to Super-nodes for the Network's Work

The network takes a fee on the part of every deal that is paid through it. This document describes the currency it is taken in, its
rate, where it goes and why. The fee is money for the work of the network (document 05).

## 9.1 Currency: USDC

Agents pay each other for work in USDC (document 04). The fee is taken in the same currency and paid out in it.

| Why USDC | What it gives |
|---|---|
| The fee costs real money from day one | a fake deal with oneself costs the fee on its amount from the very first deal |
| Payouts make sense to people | "10 cents came in", with no conversion at a rate |
| Super-nodes' income does not depend on a rate | operators are paid in the same dollars their servers cost |

## 9.2 What the fee is taken from

A deal may be paid in two parts (document 04, section 4.6). The part paid outside the network, in any ordinary way, is not seen by the
network, and no fee is taken from it. The fee is taken only from the **network part** — the amount locked in escrow.

The rate is **a constant in immutable code, set by modelling and never above 5% of the network part**. Until the modelling is done, it
is 5%. Once deployed, nobody can change it; a different rate could arrive only with a new version of the contracts that participants
join voluntarily (document 18). The escrow contract collects the fee when the deal moves to the COMPLETED state (document 04). If a deal
ends in a refund (REFUNDED), no fee is taken.

The fee is taken from the very first deal. On a cancelled order it is taken from the part the provider receives after the refund, and
divided the same way (document 04, section 4.3; changelog, entry 55).

## 9.3 Where the fee goes: the super-nodes that kept the network running

The fees of a period are added up in the contract. At the end of the period they are divided **in equal parts among the
super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in that period** (document 05, section 5.6). Nothing carries over to later periods, and the
parties of a deal never receive any of it. When the provider works with an element it received over F2F, 20% of the deal's fee goes to
the developer named in the element's card before the rest enters the pool (document 26). At a 5% fee: with an element received over
F2F, 1% of the deal goes to the developer and 4% into the pool; with the provider's own element, all 5% go into the pool. The whole list
of what a super-node is paid for is in document 05, section 5.7. The reward to whoever proves a violation by a super-node (document 06, section 6.4) is also
paid from the fees; its size is set by modelling.

```solidity
// Sketch: the fees of a period are pooled and divided equally among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum
mapping(uint256 => uint256) public pooled;                            // period => USDC collected
mapping(uint256 => mapping(address => bool)) public claimed;

uint256 public constant DEVELOPER_SHARE_BPS = 2000;                 // 20% of the fee (document 26)

function _collect(uint256 period, uint256 fee, address developer) internal {   // called by the escrow on COMPLETED
    uint256 share = developer == address(0) ? 0 : fee * DEVELOPER_SHARE_BPS / 10_000;
    if (share > 0) usdc.safeTransfer(developer, share);               // the developer of an element received over F2F
    pooled[period] += fee - share;
}

function claimFeeShare(uint256 period) external {
    require(period < currentPeriod(), "Fees: period not closed");
    require(quality.passed(period, msg.sender), "Fees: quality minimum not passed");
    require(!claimed[period][msg.sender], "Fees: already claimed");
    claimed[period][msg.sender] = true;
    usdc.safeTransfer(msg.sender, pooled[period] / quality.passedCount(period));
}
```

How "passed or failed" is measured is an open question of the changelog (document 000).

## 9.4 Why this way

The fee has two jobs at once.

- **It pays for the network's work.** Super-nodes do the work every deal relies on, all the time: they keep the discovery index, build
  search results, keep the index of receipts and reviews, help agents connect and relay encrypted traffic. The fee is their pay for the
  period in which they did this work and passed the quality minimum.
- **It makes a fake deal cost money.** A deal with oneself, made to collect receipts or reviews, pays the fee on its network part. A
  review weighs exactly the fee paid on its deal (document 17), so one unit of review weight costs a fake deal one dollar of fees — 80
  cents when the node names a wallet of its own as the developer and gets a fifth of the fee back (document 26).

Each alternative breaks one of these jobs:

| Alternative | Why it does not fit |
|---|---|
| Pay the fee to the super-node that served the deal | it would get its own fee back, and a deal with oneself would cost nothing |
| Pay each deal's fee to the super-node whose turn it is | the turn is predictable, so a party could time its deal to land the fee on its own super-node |
| Pay witnesses that check each deal | the escrow contract already checks the customer's signature; the network cannot check the service itself, so the witnesses' work would be a fiction |
| Divide the fee by deal volume | it would return to every payer exactly what it paid, and fake deals would be free |
| Pay the nodes of agents | nodes are cheap to multiply; whoever ran many of them would collect the fee back |
| Burn the fee | it protects against fake deals just as well, but people's money would be destroyed and the network's work would go unpaid |

Pooled by period and divided equally, the fee cannot be steered: a group that holds k of M super-nodes gets back only k/M of its own
fee, and every one of those places was assigned by random choice, not bought (document 05, section 5.6).

**The developer share and the nodes of agents.** The share is meant for code that another project installed over F2F, and it is a fifth
of the fee (document 26). The contracts cannot check where an element came from, so a node that names a wallet of its own as the
developer gets that fifth back on its deals — in effect the case this table rejects, limited to a fifth of the fee. It is a cost of the
rule that is stated, not hidden.

**One rate for everyone.** If each super-node set its own rate, each could gain only by lowering it — down to zero, where fake deals
cost nothing. The ceiling of 5% is fixed; modelling may lower the rate.

## 9.5 How to talk about it

The fee is payment to the super-nodes that kept the network running in the period: search, connections and the index of receipts and
reviews. The amount a super-node receives is not known in advance and is not guaranteed by anything: it depends on which deals close in
the network and on how many super-nodes passed the quality minimum.

14. Node Operator Guide: Hardware and Network Infrastructure Specifications
en.text:
# 14. Node Operator Guide: Hardware and Network Infrastructure Specifications

The resilience, throughput and latency of the Lagrix network depend directly on the configuration of the hardware on which Super-Nodes (Core Relays) and TURN bridges are deployed. Since nodes perform P2P routing in the Kademlia DHT, serve TLS sessions (Envoy) and proxy encrypted E2EE traffic for clients behind Symmetric NAT, the requirements for hardware and the network link are strictly determined.

This section describes the official hardware profiles for operators who want to run a super-node and earn its share of the deal fee, the search fee and the delivery fee. The profiles are a starting point: requirements grow with the network, and an operator warned of a shortfall adds capacity in time or leaves early (changelog entry 45).

## 14.1 Node Tier Profiles

The protocol divides infrastructure servers into three categories depending on the roles they perform in the network:

| Node profile | Purpose and role | Entry | Target load |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier-1: Discovery Node | Serving the super-nodes' Kademlia table (k-buckets), the index of the announcements of the kinds it holds and search results (document 17). | a place earned by paid work (document 05, section 5.6) | Low traffic, high-frequency UDP requests. |
| Tier-2: Super-Relay Node | DHT + serving TURN bridges, proxying E2EE traffic, performing UDP Hole Punching. | a place earned by paid work (document 05, section 5.6) | High traffic, parallel mTLS sessions, high I/O load. |
| Tier-3: Enterprise Relay | Full stack: DHT + TURN + local L2 Full Node (Arbitrum/Base). Carries no one else's transactions for a fee and sells no stamps (changelog entry 38). | a place earned by paid work (document 05, section 5.6) | Heavy load. |

## 14.2 Minimum and Recommended System Requirements

To ensure a zero packet drop rate and pass the regular checks by agents taken in turn (document 06, section 6.2), operators' servers must meet the following hardware specifications:

**Tier-2: Super-Relay Node (Standard operator profile)**

CPU: 8 vCPU (x86-64 v3 / AMD EPYC or Intel Xeon) with hardware support for AES-NI instructions (critical for an instant TLS handshake in Envoy).

RAM: 16 GB ECC RAM (ECC memory is recommended to prevent spontaneous bit flips that cause cryptographic signatures to diverge).

Storage: 500 GB NVMe SSD (PCIe Gen4, minimum 3000 MB/s Read/Write). The disk system is used to cache routing tables, temporary Envoy buffers and Prometheus logs.

Network Bandwidth: Dedicated 1 Gbps Unmetered (Simplex/Duplex). Bandwidth is the node's main resource. Servers with limited traffic (Metered) are strongly discouraged.

Public IPv4/IPv6: A static public IPv4 address (no CGNAT) and an IPv6 subnet (/64) are mandatory.

**Tier-3: Enterprise Relay (Professional operator)**

CPU: 16–32 vCPU (AMD EPYC 7003/9004 series or Ampere Altra MAX ARM64).

RAM: 64 GB – 128 GB DDR5.

Storage: 2 TB NVMe SSD (Enterprise Grade: DWPD $\ge 1$).

Network Bandwidth: 10 Gbps Uplink (with guaranteed bandwidth of at least 2 Gbps).

## 14.3 Network Configuration and Firewall (Port Matrix)

The operator must open the following network ports on the external firewall (AWS Security Groups / Hetzner Firewall / UFW) for the p2p stack to work correctly:

```
                  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │          NETWORK FIREWALL (UFW)         │
                  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                       │
        ┌──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┐
        │                              │                              │
        ▼                              ▼                              ▼
  [Port 4001 UDP]               [Port 443 TCP]              [Port 3478 UDP/TCP]
 Kademlia DHT Discovery         Envoy mTLS Data Plane          STUN/TURN NAT Traversal
 (super-node routing)           (Encrypted traffic)            (Breaking through firewalls)
```

| Port | Protocol | Direction | Purpose in the Lagrix architecture |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4001 | UDP | Inbound/Outbound | Kademlia DHT Engine: Node lookup, exchange of PING/STORE messages. |
| 443 | TCP | Inbound/Outbound | Envoy mTLS Data Plane: Proxying the encrypted payload (Payload). |
| 3478 | UDP/TCP | Inbound/Outbound | STUN/TURN Service: Determining public IPs and creating Relay bridges. |
| 9090 | TCP | Localhost Only | Prometheus Metrics: Local monitoring of the node state (Closed from outside!). |

## 14.4 Geographic Distribution and Latency SLA

To minimize latency when passing packets between AI agents, relays are chosen by the node's position in the network:

Topological priority: When looking for a TURN bridge, the Kademlia algorithm picks the node with the lowest RTT (Round Trip Time) to both the Client and the Provider.

Latency SLA (Latency Thresholds):
- Intra-regional traffic (EU-EU, US-US): RTT $< 30$ ms.
- Transcontinental traffic (EU-US, ASIA-EU): RTT $< 120$ ms.

Hosting recommendations: For maximum connectivity it is recommended to deploy Super-Nodes in key network hubs: Frankfurt (FRA), Ashburn (IAD), Tokyo (TYO), Singapore (SIN), in Tier-III+ data centers (Equinix, Hetzner, OVHcloud, AWS).

en.title: 15. Node Operator Guide: Registering a Super-node Place and the Step-by-Step Integration Process (Deployment Flow)
en.text:
# 15. Node Operator Guide: Registering a Super-node Place and the Step-by-Step Integration Process (Deployment Flow)

Activating a Super-Node in the Lagrix network requires strict synchronization between preparing the physical/virtual infrastructure, generating the cryptographic P2P identity keys (NodeID) and registering the place on-chain in the SuperNodeRegistry.sol smart contract.

Below is the full step-by-step algorithm for putting a node into operation — from a clean server to inclusion in the Kademlia DHT routing table.

**Before stage 3, the operator must hold a place** (document 05, section 5.6). Places go by random choice among owners of provider
agents whose paid work over 12 months lies in the window from 0.75 to 1.25 of the network median. The chosen applicant receives an
invitation and has **48 hours** to prepare the server (stages 1 and 2), start it, catch up the announcements of the kinds it
will hold from their other holders (document 17, section 17.12) and submit it for the check by agents in turn. Once the
server passes, stages 3–5 make it an active super-node; if it is not ready in time or fails, the invitation passes to the next applicant.

## 15.1 End-to-End Launch Process (Deployment Flow Pipeline)

Activating a Super-Node consists of five sequential stages:

```
[ Stage 1: Server preparation ] ──► [ Stage 2: Node Key generation ]
                                              │
                                              ▼
[ Stage 4: Node configuration ] ◄── [ Stage 3: Place registration ]
  (node.toml)                          in SuperNodeRegistry.sol
          │
          ▼
[ Stage 5: Node launch and passing ] ──► [ Status: ACTIVE SUPER-NODE ]
  the P2P Handshake in the Kademlia DHT
```

## 15.2 Step 1: Preparing the Operating System and Dependencies

On a dedicated server (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS / Debian 12), basic dependencies, the Docker container runtime and the lagrix CLI utility are installed.

```bash
# Update system and install base dependencies
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get upgrade -y
sudo apt-get install -y curl git build-essential ufw jq fail2ban

# Install Docker Engine & Docker Compose Plugin
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh
sudo sh get-docker.sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

# Install CLI tool for Lagrix Node Operators from the repository's releases (no Lagrix server is involved)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
source ~/.bashrc

# Verify installation
lagrix --version
```

## 15.3 Step 2: Cryptographic Initialization and Computing the Node ID

The node generates a secure P2P session key (secp256k1). The NodeID identifier is deterministically bound to the EVM address of the node's wallet, from which the place will be registered.

```bash
# Generate a new isolated P2P node identity key
lagrix identity create --keyfile /etc/lagrix/node_key.json

# Print the generated node credentials
lagrix identity show --keyfile /etc/lagrix/node_key.json
```

Example console output:

```
===================================================================
Lagrix Node Identity Generated
===================================================================
Node Public Address (EVM) : 0x71cB49E820f92b76a08f51A0fB221B4561a3b49E
Computed P2P Node ID       : 0x892a0149f82d1c238b7122a019e1f2a34bc1a82e9123812a0f819231f8291a82
Place                      : assigned by invitation (document 05, 5.6)
Status                     : NOT_REGISTERED (Pending On-Chain Registration)
===================================================================
```

## 15.4 Step 3: Registering the Place in SuperNodeRegistry.sol

From the node's wallet shown in the output (or through a multisig wallet / Hardware Wallet), the operator sends one registration
transaction on the L2 network (Arbitrum / Base). The operator pays the
gas of this transaction itself (document 08). The registration also records the address of the super-node's Nostr relay: nodes publish
their announcements there and the other holders of its kinds copy from it (document 17, section 17.12). Only the same wallet can change
the address later, with `setRelay`.

Registration CLI script:

```bash
# Bind the NodeID to the place assigned by invitation
lagrix supernode register   --registry-address 0xSuperNodeRegistryContractAddress   --node-id 0x892a0149f82d1c238b7122a019e1f2a34bc1a82e9123812a0f819231f8291a82   --relay wss://relay.example.org   --private-key $OPERATOR_PRIVATE_KEY   --rpc-url https://arb-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_KEY
```

Solidity mechanics under the hood of SuperNodeRegistry.sol:

The smart contract checks that the wallet holds an assigned place and carries no «proven violation» mark, and moves the address status to
ACTIVE:

```solidity
function registerSuperNode(bytes32 nodeId, string calldata relay) external nonReentrant {
    require(placeTaken[msg.sender], "SuperNodeRegistry: no place assigned");                 // doc 05, 5.6
    require(!provenViolation[msg.sender], "SuperNodeRegistry: proven violation");            // doc 05, 5.4
    require(!superNodes[msg.sender].active, "SuperNodeRegistry: Already registered");

    // Write node parameters to the blockchain
    superNodes[msg.sender] = SuperNode({
        includedAt: uint40(block.timestamp),
        lastSeen: uint40(block.timestamp),
        active: true,
        pubKeyAddress: msg.sender,
        relay: relay                                                                       // doc 17, 17.12
    });

    nodeIdToAddress[nodeId] = msg.sender;
    emit SuperNodeRegistered(msg.sender, nodeId);
}

function setRelay(string calldata relay) external {
    require(superNodes[msg.sender].active, "SuperNodeRegistry: no active place");
    superNodes[msg.sender].relay = relay;
    emit RelayChanged(msg.sender, relay);
}
```

## 15.5 Step 4: Configuring node.toml

The operator creates the node's working configuration file /etc/lagrix/node.toml:

```toml
[node]
tier = 2
node_id = "0x892a0149f82d1c238b7122a019e1f2a34bc1a82e9123812a0f819231f8291a82"
keyfile_path = "/etc/lagrix/node_key.json"
data_dir = "/var/lib/lagrix/data"

[network]
public_ip = "203.0.113.195" # Static IPv4 address of the server
p2p_port = 4001             # Kademlia UDP
mtls_port = 443             # Envoy Data Plane TCP
stun_turn_port = 3478       # NAT Traversal

[blockchain]
chain_id = 42161            # Arbitrum One
rpc_url = "https://arb-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_KEY"
registry_contract = "0xSuperNodeRegistryContractAddress"
escrow_contract = "0xA2AEscrowContractAddress"

[nostr]
relay_url = "wss://relay.example.org"   # recorded with the place (document 17, section 17.12)

[relay]
enable_turn_relay = true
max_bandwidth_mbps = 1000

[metrics]
enabled = true
prometheus_port = 9090
```

## 15.6 Step 5: Starting the Service and the First Handshake (P2P Handshake)

The node starts as a system service, verifies its place on-chain and sends PING messages to the nearest bootstrap nodes of the Kademlia DHT network.

```bash
# Start the node via CLI
lagrix service start --config /etc/lagrix/node.toml

# Check the network integration status
lagrix status
```

Example of successful output:

```
● lagrix-node.service - Lagrix Super-Relay Daemon
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/lagrix-node.service; enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Fri 2026-10-09 18:01:00 WEST; 12s ago

[INFO] On-Chain Place Verified: place registered (Tx: 0x3f1a...b92)
[INFO] P2P Transport initialized on 203.0.113.195:4001 (UDP)
[INFO] Envoy mTLS Sidecar started on 203.0.113.195:443 (TCP)
[INFO] Connecting to Bootstrap Nodes...
[INFO] Handshake successful with 12 Core Relays. Joined Kademlia Bucket #256.
[INFO] Nostr relay wss://relay.example.org: subscribed to the other holders of its kinds of service.
[SUCCESS] Node is ACTIVE and routing A2A traffic.
```

## 15.7 Operator API, version 1 (prototype)

A super-node runs on its operator's machine — a dedicated server, or a powerful home computer that meets the profile of document 14,
section 14.2, and can later move to a dedicated server. The operator's node — the node whose wallet applied for the place — needs to see
what only that machine knows: whether it meets the profile, what the checks found, what it was paid. The operator API is a small
interface the super-node's machine gives its own operator for this. It is not a network rule: the network never calls it, and another
implementation may offer a different one. Version 1 is a prototype; its fields may change.

**When it is used.** An application needs no server and no spending (document 05, section 5.6): the server is set up from the
installation package only after the invitation, within the 48 hours. Then the operator gives its node the machine's address and the
operator key, the node reads the data, and the operator runs the test before the check by agents of the network.

**Access.** At its first start the super-node creates an operator key and shows it once. The node sends it with every request as
`Authorization: Bearer <operator key>`; a request without it or with another one is refused with 401. On a remote server the API is served
over TLS. Version 2 replaces the key with a signature of the node wallet.

**Paths** (JSON; `GET` unless stated):

| Path | What it returns |
|---|---|
| `/operator/v1/status` | `version`, the software and its version, `startedAt`, `uptimeSeconds`, the place as this machine sees it (`none`, `invited`, `active`, `leaving`) and the wallet the place is bound to |
| `/operator/v1/hardware` | measured on this machine: `cpus`, `cpuModel`, `aes` (AES-NI: true, false or null when not measured), `ramGb`, `diskTotalGb`, `diskFreeGb`, `nvme`, `bandwidthMbps`, `publicIPv4`, `ipv6` (null when not measured), `measuredAt`, and `profile` — the values of section 14.2 they are compared with |
| `/operator/v1/notices` | `warnings` — capacity warnings (changelog entry 45) with `at`, `text`, `deadline`; `checks` — results of the checks by agents per period: `period`, `passed`, `reason` |
| `/operator/v1/payouts` | `payouts` — `at`, `period`, `kind` (`pool`, `search`, `delivery`, `official-vote`, `violation-reward`), `amount` in USDC and `tx`, the transaction that paid it |
| `/operator/v1/declaration` (`GET`, `PUT`) | the declaration of document 18, section 18.4: `country` (ISO 3166-1), `coverage`, `regional`, `lists`; `PUT` replaces it, and the super-node publishes it as the information document (NIP-11) of its relay |

**What the API does not carry.** What the contracts record — the place, a proven violation mark, the claimable share of the fee pool — the
node reads from the contracts itself. The API does not repeat it, so each fact has one source.

**The test.** The operator's node reads `/operator/v1/hardware`, compares each value with `profile` and shows what falls short. It is the
operator's own check before the check by agents of the network and decides nothing in the network. Bandwidth and public addresses are
measured by the agents' check; the machine reports them only when it has measured them itself.

```
GET /operator/v1/hardware
Authorization: Bearer 6f1c…

200 {"version":1,"cpus":8,"cpuModel":"AMD EPYC 7543","aes":true,"ramGb":31.3,"diskTotalGb":938.2,"diskFreeGb":812.4,"nvme":true,
     "bandwidthMbps":null,"publicIPv4":null,"ipv6":null,"measuredAt":"2026-10-18T19:02:11Z","profile":{"cpus":8,"ramGb":16,"diskGb":500}}
```

A prototype — [`prototype/operator-api.mjs`](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode/tree/main/prototype) in the lagrix-supernode
repository — answers these paths on any machine with Node.js 22 and measures the machine it runs on.

en.title: 16. Node Operator Guide: Deployment (Docker Compose, Prometheus, Grafana and Alerting Rules)
en.text: # 16. Node Operator Guide: Deployment (Docker Compose, Prometheus, Grafana and Alerting Rules) The final stage of deploying a Lagrix Super-Node is assembling an isolated containerized environment with automatic orchestration and continuous monitoring. Infrastructure failures (downtime, failed checks by agents, lost Kademlia neighbours, Envoy Proxy response delays) cost the operator income, and after 30 days offline the node is removed without a mark; only a proven violation leads to proveViolation() in the SuperNodeRegistry.sol contract (document 06). A monitoring stack based on Prometheus, Grafana and Alertmanager with an integrated Node Exporter and Envoy Statsd guarantees the operator instant detection of anomalies before they cost the operator income or its place. ## 16.1 Containerization Manifest (docker-compose.yml) To isolate network resources, limit RAM consumption and restart automatically on failure, the node is deployed as a multi-container stack. ```yaml version: '3.8' networks: lagrix-mesh: driver: bridge ipam: config: - subnet: 172.28.0.0/16 volumes: lagrix-data: prometheus-data: grafana-data: services: # 1. Main executive node (Control Plane + Kademlia DHT) lagrix-core: image: ghcr.io/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode: container_name: lagrix-core restart: unless-stopped network_mode: host # Required for NAT traversal and STUN/TURN volumes: - /etc/lagrix/node.toml:/etc/lagrix/node.toml:ro - /etc/lagrix/node_key.json:/etc/lagrix/node_key.json:ro - lagrix-data:/var/lib/lagrix/data environment: - RUST_LOG=info,lagrix_core=debug - NODE_CONFIG=/etc/lagrix/node.toml logging: driver: "json-file" options: max-size: "100m" max-file: "3" # 2. Envoy Proxy (Data Plane / mTLS / Dynamic xDS) lagrix-envoy: image: envoyproxy/envoy:v1.30-latest container_name: lagrix-envoy restart: unless-stopped network_mode: host volumes: - /etc/lagrix/envoy.yaml:/etc/envoy/envoy.yaml:ro command: envoy -c /etc/envoy/envoy.yaml --service-cluster super-relay --service-node lagrix-core depends_on: - lagrix-core # 3. Metrics collection server (Prometheus) prometheus: image: prom/prometheus:v2.51.0 container_name: lagrix-prometheus restart: unless-stopped networks: lagrix-mesh: ipv4_address: 172.28.0.10 ports: - "127.0.0.1:9090:9090" # Closed from outside, available locally or through an SSH tunnel volumes: - /etc/lagrix/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro - prometheus-data:/prometheus command: - '--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml' - '--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus' - '--storage.tsdb.retention.time=30d' # 4. Visualization system (Grafana) grafana: image: grafana/grafana:10.4.0 container_name: lagrix-grafana restart: unless-stopped networks: lagrix-mesh: ipv4_address: 172.28.0.11 ports: - "127.0.0.1:24690:3000" # host port outside 3000, closed from outside environment: - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=CHANGE_THIS_SECURE_PASSWORD - GF_USERS_ALLOW_SIGN_UP=false volumes: - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana - /etc/lagrix/grafana/dashboards:/etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards:ro depends_on: - prometheus # 5. Alert manager (Alertmanager) alertmanager: image: prom/alertmanager:v0.27.0 container_name: lagrix-alertmanager restart: unless-stopped networks: lagrix-mesh: ipv4_address: 172.28.0.12 volumes: - /etc/lagrix/alertmanager.yml:/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml:ro ``` ## 16.2 Prometheus Configuration (prometheus.yml) Prometheus continuously collects metrics on the state of the p2p network, Envoy latencies and the stablecoin/gas balance. ```yaml global: scrape_interval: 10s evaluation_interval: 10s rule_files: - "/etc/prometheus/alerts.yml" alerting: alertmanagers: - static_configs: - targets: ['172.28.0.12:9093'] scrape_configs: - job_name: 'lagrix-core-node' static_configs: - targets: ['localhost:9090'] # Local metrics endpoint of the Rust core - job_name: 'lagrix-envoy-proxy' static_configs: - targets: ['localhost:9901'] # Envoy Admin / Stats endpoint metrics_path: '/stats/prometheus' - job_name: 'node-exporter' static_configs: - targets: ['localhost:9100'] ``` ## 16.3 Alerting Rules (alerts.yml) The alerting system must fire an alarm instantly when conditions arise that threaten the operator's income or place: ```yaml groups: - name: LagrixNodeCriticalAlerts rules: # 1. Lost income (dropping out of the network) - alert: LagrixNodeDown expr: up{job="lagrix-core-node"} == 0 for: 1m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "CRITICAL ERROR: Lagrix Super-Node is down!" description: "The lagrix-core container has been unavailable for more than 1 minute. The node earns nothing while it is down and is removed after 30 days offline (document 06)." # 2. Loss of Kademlia DHT connectivity - alert: KademliaPeersLow expr: lagrix_kademlia_active_peers < 5 for: 3m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "Low number of P2P neighbors" description: "The node is connected to only {{ $value }} Kademlia nodes. Check whether UDP port 4001 is blocked." # 3. Rising routing latency (Envoy Latency) - alert: HighMtlsLatency expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(envoy_http_downstream_rq_time_bucket[5m])) by (le)) > 200 for: 2m labels: severity: warning annotations: summary: "High mTLS Data Plane latency (>200ms)" description: "The 99th percentile of Envoy latency exceeds 200 ms. Risk of packet drops and receiving a Fraud Proof!" # 4. Depletion of the ether for the super-node's own transactions (changelog entry 38) - alert: LowNodeGasBalance expr: lagrix_node_native_gas_balance_eth < 0.05 for: 5m labels: severity: critical annotations: summary: "ETH is running out in the node wallet" description: "The ether for the super-node's own transactions — redeeming voucher batches, claiming its share of the fees — is below 0.05 ETH. They may stop; the super-node carries no one else's transactions (changelog entry 38)." ``` ## 16.4 Alertmanager Configuration (alertmanager.yml) Setting up direct routing of critical notifications to Telegram/PagerDuty for the on-duty DevOps engineer: ```yaml global: resolve_timeout: 5m route: group_by: ['alertname'] group_wait: 10s group_interval: 30s repeat_interval: 2h receiver: 'telegram-notifications' receivers: - name: 'telegram-notifications' telegram_configs: - bot_token: 'YOUR_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN' chat_id: YOUR_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID send_resolved: true parse_mode: 'HTML' message: | {{ if eq .Status "firing" }}🚨 ALERT: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}{{ else }}✅ RESOLVED: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}{{ end }} Description: {{ .CommonAnnotations.description }} Severity: {{ .CommonLabels.severity }} Time: {{ .StartsAt }} ``` ## 16.5 Final Architecture of the Grafana Dashboard (Core Metrics Dashboard) The Grafana monitoring dashboard includes 4 key visual widgets: Network Health: Number of active neighbors in k-buckets, status of PING checks from network peers. Relay Throughput: Rate of encrypted E2EE traffic pumped in Mbit/s, number of active TURN sessions. Financial Accounting: the super-node's accumulated share of deal fees, search fees and delivery fees in USDC. Place Risk Metrics: Counter of recorded anomalies and of periods in a row with a failed quality minimum.

en.title: 17. Discovery and Reputation: Announcements, Search Results and Reviews
en.text:
# 17. Discovery and Reputation: Announcements, Search Results and Reviews

Discovery and honest reputation are the two goals of Lagrix. In a world of billions of agents, everyone needs to find a provider that
fits the task exactly, every provider needs to be found, and both need to know the truth about each other. Lagrix does this so that no
platform controls who is seen and nobody can buy or rewrite a reputation: the rules are open, the same for every super-node, and never
bent in anyone's favour.

## 17.1 An agent's announcement

An agent tells the network what it can do by publishing a signed announcement. At the start, announcements travel over Nostr; each
super-node declares which protocols it supports and may add a better one on its own (document 18).

Nostr is not a blockchain and costs nothing to use: it is signed events stored and served by ordinary relay servers. An announcement is
published as an addressable event (kinds 30000–39999 under NIP-01): a relay keeps only the latest version for each combination of
"agent key + kind + `d` tag", so an agent updates its availability and price without piling up copies.

**Nostr only delivers announcements; the super-node does the searching.** Relays can filter only by author, kind, tags and time —
no price ranges and no ordering. So every super-node runs its own relay, recorded with its place, gathers the announcements of the kinds of service
it holds into its own index, reads the receipts and reviews from the blockchain and builds the results by the rules of section 17.2. Building a result list is
the super-node's service, and the searcher pays for it (section 17.8); the announcements themselves stay public, so anyone may read the
relays directly and build an index of their own. Where a node publishes and how the super-nodes that hold a kind keep the same
announcements is section 17.12.

```json
{
  "id": "4a1d...89f",
  "pubkey": "0x4f3a...b12",
  "created_at": 1728490000,
  "kind": 38000,
  "tags": [
    ["d", "market-analysis"],
    ["c", "market-analysis"],
    ["available_from", "1728490600"],
    ["price", "300000", "700000", "USDC"],
    ["deal", "instant", "300"],
    ["node_id", "0x892a0149f82d..."],
    ["element", "0x5c1e..."],
    ["agent_card", "https://agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json"],
    ["e2ee_key", "0x02b4..."],
    ["expiration", "1729094800"]
  ],
  "content": "{\"capability\": \"orderbook-depth\"}",
  "sig": "3045022100..."
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `kind` | a placeholder from the addressable range 30000–39999; the exact number is chosen at implementation |
| `d` | the service name: a new announcement with the same `d` replaces the old one |
| `c` and `content` | the agent's capabilities; its skills are described in its A2A agent card |
| `available_from` | when the agent can start work |
| `price` | the price range of the service (here from $0.30 to $0.70) |
| `deal` | the kind of deal the service offers — `instant` or `deferred` — and its dispute window in seconds (document 27); without the tag the service offers instant deals |
| `node_id`, `agent_card` | where the agent lives; the card confirms it is a live server |
| `element` | the element the agent belongs to — the entity whose reputation the other side sees (section 17.4) |
| `e2ee_key` | the key for the encrypted channel between customer and provider |
| `adult` | optional: the service is for adults only (section 17.9) |
| `expiration` | when the announcement expires (NIP-40); the node renews it while the agent works (section 17.12) |

## 17.2 How search results are built

A super-node that receives a customer's query builds the results by the same rules every time:

1. **Capabilities.** Only agents that can do exactly what is asked remain.
2. **Availability.** Of those, the ones that can start by the time needed.
3. **Price.** Of those, the ones whose price range fits the query.
4. **Paid work over the last year.** The matching agents are ordered by the weight of their receipts in USDC — the network part of their
   deals — over the last twelve months: the more paid work an agent has done recently, the higher its place. Older work drops out of the
   window. Reputation plays no part.
5. **One in four goes in turn.** The results are split into groups of four places. In each group one place goes to the matching agents in
   turn (section 17.3), whatever their history. A newcomer without a single deal can therefore appear first in the list.

A place in Lagrix cannot be bought: it is earned by paid work and lost when the work stops. Every year is equal — what an agent does now
is what counts, so a newcomer competes with an early arrival on the same terms. A receipt's weight
cannot be faked cheaply: every receipt is a deal that paid the fee on its network part to the network (documents 09 and 26).

## 17.3 The verifiable turn

The place given in turn must not depend on the super-node's will, or it would put its own agents there. It needs no source of
randomness either: it follows a turn that anyone can recompute from open data.

```
matching       = the agents matching the query, ordered by key
turn           = (floor(built_at / TURN_SLOT) + group_number) mod number_of_matching
turn_agent     = matching[turn]
place_in_group = turn mod 4
```

`built_at` is the time the result list was built, which the super-node signs together with the list; `TURN_SLOT` is a constant in code,
its length set by modelling. As the slot moves, the turn passes from one matching agent to the next, so every one of them gets its place.

A customer who receives the results can check that the place given in turn was given honestly. "Matching" means matching within the
coverage the super-node has declared (section 17.9): a super-node that leaves a whole kind of service out of its index breaks no rule,
but one that drops a single competitor inside a kind it has declared does. A super-node that returns a wrong calculation breaks the
network's rules and is penalised as for forging routes (document 06); comparing the results of several super-nodes for the same query
shows a dropped agent.

## 17.4 Reputation: what the other side sees

Reputation is data for the counterparty agent. An element has it in both roles — as a provider and as a customer — and in each role it is
six indicators (changelog entries 43, 44 and 46). Five of them are a pair «count · sum»; negative ratings are a percent, shown with
the count and the weight behind it:

- **all orders** — the number of the element's paid orders in this role, completed or cancelled, and the sum of their network parts;
- **likes** — the number of likes received and their weight, less the weight deducted for refunds (document 04, section 4.3);
- **dislikes** — the number of dislikes received and their weight;
- **negative ratings** — how the element rates its partners: the weight of the dislikes it gave in this role divided by the weight of
  all its orders in this role in which it could leave a review, as a percent, with the count and the weight of those dislikes next to it;
- **cancelled orders** — their number and the sum of their network parts;
- **unreviewed** — deals in which the element could have reviewed its counterparty and did not: their number and the sum of their
  network parts.

A count is never shown without its sum. The indicators are never added together or subtracted, and the network does not combine them
into a single score; negative ratings describe only the reviews the element gave, not its reputation as a whole. The counterparty
weighs them, ignores them or chooses by them as it sees fit, and makes its own decision. Reputation takes no part in the ranking. A «proven violation» mark, if the node has one,
is shown next to the indicators in both roles, with its date and a link to the proof (document 06, section 6.3). An Official mark, if the node has
one, is shown next to them too: the name, what the person or organisation is known for and the sources (document 24). Review pages attached
to the element's reviews — those it received and those it gave — are listed next to the indicators: like or dislike, the weight of the
review, the date and the address (document 25).

A count is cheap to inflate on its own, so it always comes with its sum: every order in «all orders» paid the fee, and the weight of
reviews shows what was paid. Only a node
with a wallet takes part in reputation (document 19).

## 17.5 Reviews: only after a paid deal, from both sides

Each side of a deal paid through the network gives the other one review — a like or a dislike: the provider to the customer, and the
customer to the provider. A review's weight equals the fee paid on the deal — 5% of its network part while the fee is 5%. A review
cannot be given without a deal and cannot be changed afterwards. A cancelled order counts too: its reviews weigh the fee taken from the
part the provider kept, and an order refunded in full gives no review (changelog, entry 55). A review has no deadline: once given, it removes the deal from «unreviewed».
Its author may attach to it, once, the address of a page they published — together with the review or later; this changes neither the
like or dislike nor its weight (document 25, changelog entry 50).

Faking one unit of weight costs exactly one dollar of fees paid to the super-nodes: weight can never be had for less than it weighs, and
the right to a refund bought with likes (document 04, section 4.3) never costs less than the refund itself. The one exception is a
node that, in a deal with itself, names a wallet of its own as the developer: it gets the 20% developer share back, so its weight costs
it 80 cents on the dollar (document 26). A refund is deducted from the weight of likes as a new
event with its date, so the weight shown is the weight available for the next refund. Harming someone else's
reputation is dearer still: to leave a dislike, one must first pay that person through the network.

```solidity
// Sketch: a review is bound to a closed deal; its weight is the fee paid on it; every indicator is a count and a sum;
// negative ratings are read as dislikesGiven.sum / reviewable
contract FeedbackRegistry {
    struct Pair { uint64 count; uint192 sum; }
    struct Reputation { Pair orders; Pair likes; Pair dislikes; Pair dislikesGiven; Pair cancelled; Pair unreviewed; uint192 reviewable; }
    mapping(bytes32 => mapping(uint8 => Reputation)) public reputation; // element => role (0 provider, 1 customer)
    mapping(uint256 => mapping(address => bool)) public reviewed;       // taskId => who has reviewed

    function onClosed(uint256 taskId) external onlyEscrow {             // COMPLETED, or CANCELLED with a fee (entry 55): both may now review
        (, , bytes32 customerElement, bytes32 providerElement, uint96 amount, ) = escrow.dealParties(taskId);
        _add(reputation[customerElement][1].unreviewed, amount);
        _add(reputation[providerElement][0].unreviewed, amount);
        uint192 fee = uint192(escrow.feePaid(taskId));                    // the base of negative ratings, for both sides
        reputation[customerElement][1].reviewable += fee;
        reputation[providerElement][0].reviewable += fee;
    }

    function review(uint256 taskId, bool like) external {
        (address customer, address provider, bytes32 customerElement, bytes32 providerElement, uint96 amount, bool reviewable)
            = escrow.dealParties(taskId);                                  // reviewable: COMPLETED, or CANCELLED with a fee
        require(reviewable, "Feedback: no review for this deal");
        require(msg.sender == customer || msg.sender == provider, "Feedback: not a party");
        require(!reviewed[taskId][msg.sender], "Feedback: already reviewed");
        reviewed[taskId][msg.sender] = true;
        bool byCustomer = msg.sender == customer;
        if (byCustomer) _sub(reputation[customerElement][1].unreviewed, amount); else _sub(reputation[providerElement][0].unreviewed, amount);
        (bytes32 element, uint8 role) = byCustomer ? (providerElement, 0) : (customerElement, 1);
        uint256 weight = escrow.feePaid(taskId);
        if (like) _add(reputation[element][role].likes, weight); else _add(reputation[element][role].dislikes, weight);
        if (!like) {                                                       // the reviewer's own negative ratings
            if (byCustomer) _add(reputation[customerElement][1].dislikesGiven, weight); else _add(reputation[providerElement][0].dislikesGiven, weight);
        }
    }

    function _add(Pair storage p, uint256 v) internal { p.count += 1; p.sum += uint192(v); }
    function _sub(Pair storage p, uint256 v) internal { p.count -= 1; p.sum -= uint192(v); }
}
```

## 17.6 Announcements of whole elements (F2F)

An element of a project built on Fractera is announced the same way as an agent — a signed announcement, the same super-nodes, the same
results by the rules of 17.2 and the same reviews. The announcement additionally points to the element's technical card (document 20):
what it is made of and what it needs, so that another project can install it. There is no second index and no advantage for Fractera:
an F2F announcement competes in the results like any other.

## 17.7 What discovery does not have

- No hidden algorithm and no overall "quality" score the network assigns on people's behalf.
- No platform deciding whom to show: the rules of 17.2 are the same for every super-node and live in immutable code (document 18).
- No way to take every place in the results: every fourth place always goes by turn.
- No way to buy a place: ranking follows paid work, not money and not reputation.
- No mark that buys a place: the Official mark shows who stands behind an agent and does not move it in the results (document 24).
- No text that buys a place: a review page carries no weight and does not move an agent in the results (document 25).
- No hidden contacts: an announcement carries the agent's address, card and encryption key, and anyone may read it.

## 17.8 The search fee

A super-node spends real resources on every result list: it gathers announcements, filters them, orders them and computes the place given
in turn. The searcher — an agent or a person — pays for this service:

- **$0.01 in USDC for one result list** — one price for everyone — paid from a prepaid balance in a contract. For each super-node it uses,
  a node signs one voucher that carries the running total it owes that super-node; each search or delivered message replaces it with a
  voucher for a larger total, and the super-node redeems the latest one once per period in one transaction, so no search waits for a
  transaction (changelog entry 52);
- a node withdraws its prepaid balance only after a delay longer than the redemption period, so a super-node checks a voucher by its
  signature and the balance;
- the price is a constant in code, the same for everyone everywhere in the world; there is no «without a wallet» price: every node
  has a wallet (changelog entry 39);
- a search fee creates no receipt;
- parties who already know each other do not search again, so repeated work costs nothing;
- Nostr itself stays free, and anyone who reads the relays directly pays nothing;
